As discussed in Sec. V, the parameter space identified in Eq. (54) for each one of these CSLs corresponds to a 2D surface, with no symmetry-breaking phase transition detected in Monte Carlo simulations down to the lowest temperatures, as we shall discuss in Sec. VII below. At low temperatures, effective Gauss’s laws are imposed on an emergent rank-2 field constructed in terms of the 𝖤\mathsf{E}, 𝖳2\mathsf{T}_{2}, and 𝖳1,−\mathsf{T}_{1,-} irreps. This is the case for any point in the parameter space characterizing these two CSLs. However, it is crucial to realize that, although the form of the effective gauge theory remains the same, the precise constituents of the rank-2 field expressed in terms of spins do differ. Such variation is captured by the dependence of the rank-2 tensor on the parameters {vi±,vp±}\{v_{i\pm},v_{p\pm}\} that define the 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}} irrep [Eqs. (6,7)]. Indeed, by tuning the constituents of the rank-2 fields, we are also effectively tuning the definition of the charge in these spin liquids. Consequently, one may understand the 2D spin liquid manifolds as a continuous set of models where the 𝖳𝟣,±\mathsf{T_{1,\pm}} of the low-energy emergent gauge fields are smoothly evolving as a function of Jz±J_{z\pm}, while the full gauge fields are constrained to fulfill a set of Gauss’s laws.

Having discussed how the effective gauge theories describing the CSL 6 and the CSL 7 smoothly evolve as the microscopic Hamiltonian parameters are modified while keeping the system in one of these two CSLs, we now turn to consider how these two CSLs are connected to each other. Figure 5 illustrates a phase diagram where the region of stability of multiple CSLs is shown. There, we take Jz​zJ_{zz} and Jz±J_{z\pm} to be free parameters while (J±,J±⁣±)(J_{\pm},J_{\pm\pm}) are fixed by Eq. (54). We first note that the two parameter spaces defining the CSL 6 and CSL 7 meet on the line defined by {Jz​z,J±,J±⁣±,Jz±}={J,J/6,J/3,0}\{J_{zz},J_{\pm},J_{\pm\pm},J_{z\pm}\}=\{J,J/6,J/3,0\} with J>0J>0. This line, shown as the white dashed line in Fig. 5, corresponds to the CSL 5 [66], where the rank-2 fields decompose into one rank-2 field and one rank-1 field, each fulfilling an independent Gauss’s law. In particular, for the CSL 6, the gauge field 𝑬𝖲𝖵{\bf\it E}^{\mathsf{SV}} in Eq. (57) and the Gauss’s laws in Eqs. (55)-(56) decompose into the rank-1 𝑬𝗂𝖼𝖾{\bf\it E}^{\mathsf{ice}} and the rank-2 𝑬𝖳𝟣+𝖤{\bf\it E}^{\mathsf{T_{1}+E}} electric fields constrained by the Gauss’s laws in Eq. (53). Importantly, this is the limit of vanishing Jz±J_{z\pm} which characterizes non-Kramers ions discussed in Sec. IV 88 8 Here we note that the {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters corresponding to the CLS 5 in Fig. 5 are such that the ratio Jz​z:J±:J±⁣±=6:1:2J_{zz}:J_{\pm}:J_{\pm\pm}=6:1:2 is always fulfilled therefore identifying a 1D region as a function of Jz​zJ_{zz} as illustrated in Fig. 5. The evolution of these parameters on that boundary is given by the parametrization of the CSLs 6 and 7, Eqs. (54) and  (62), while setting Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0..

The other boundaries of the CSL 6 and 7 parameter spaces are located at Jz​z=−|12​Jz±|J_{zz}=-\left|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}J_{z\pm}\right| with Jz±J_{z\pm} positive for the CSL 6 while it is negative for the CSL 7. These two boundaries correspond to the CSL 8 (for Jz±>0J_{z\pm}>0), and CSL 9 (for Jz±<0J_{z\pm}<0), respectively. These boundaries, marked by solid white lines in Fig. 5, separate the CSL 6 and 7 from the A2A_{2} (all-in/all-out, AIAO) magnetically ordered phase. As discussed at the beginning of this section, the CSLs 8 and 9, “viewed” as the boundary of CSLs 6 and 7 with the magnetically ordered 𝖠𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}} phase, have a higher degeneracy. The CSL 8 and 9 are thus CSLs with a higher number of low-energy-fluctuating DOFs [Eq. (65)], and contain all of the fluctuating DOFs of the CSLs 6 and 7 [Eq. (55)], respectively.

We have now discussed how the CSLs 6 and 7 display a smoothly varying definition of their electric field subject to the emergent Gauss’s laws, and how they are connected to other CSLs on the boundary within the parameter space that define them. From an experimental context, such a change in the electric field can be exposed via the equal time polarized and unpolarized neutron structure factors which evolve as a function of the Jz±J_{z\pm} and Jz​zJ_{zz} coupling parameters. Figure 6 illustrates the spin structure factor, unpolarized and polarized (spin flipping (SF) channel and non-spin flipping (NSF) channel) neutron structure factor in the (h​k​0)(hk0) plane for five different sets of parameters marked by yellow crosses in Fig. 5, which correspond to CSLs 9, 7, 5, 6, 8, in this respective order. The data illustrated here was obtained using a large-𝒩\mathcal{N} approximation which yields qualitatively similar results to those obtained with CMC simulations, except for the case with Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 in the T→0T\to 0 limit which displays disorder-by-disorder selection of a spin ice ground state [66]. In this figure, and heretofore, we have considered an isotropic gg tensor assuming that the fluctuations in all spin components are taken on equal footing in generating the neutron scattering structure factor [66, 96]. We refer the reader to Appendix D for the explicit definition of these correlation functions and for a short discussion regarding the choice of an isotropic gg tensor used in these calculations. For the CSLs 5, 6 and 7, their effective gauge theories are characterized by an emergent Gauss’s law of a rank-2 electric field. The latter is responsible for the presence of four-fold pinch points in the correlation functions, besides the familiar two-fold pinch points, see Fig. 6 where white circles (squares) in the unpolarized neutron structure factor (polarized NSF channel) indicate the location of two-fold (four-fold) pinch points. Although these anisotropic features remain observable in the structure factors, the overall intensity distribution significantly changes reflecting the evolving nature of the gauge fields and their functional dependence on the parametrization used in Fig. 5.

Rather importantly, we note that the CSL 9 (HAFM*) also exhibits four-fold pinch points in its neutron structure factor at the Γ\Gamma point, although its Gauss’s law is not associated with a higher-rank field. This four-fold pinch point is instead the consequence of the neutron (magnetic moment) scattering transverse projector  [108], which is non-analytical at the Γ\Gamma point, and is not caused by an emergent gauge structure of the model. We therefore note that, although the observation of four-fold pinch points is often a strong indication of an emergent higher-rank gauge theory, when observed at the Γ\Gamma point, it is strictly neither a necessary nor a sufficient condition for the identification of such an underlying gauge theory 99 9 We note that the CSL 5 exhibits a four-fold pinch point at (020)(020) and symmetry-related points in its unpolarized neutron structure factors shown in the third row of Fig. 6. The spin structure factor of the same model, only shows two-fold pinch points at this qq-point. These four-fold pinch points are produced by the combination of two overlapping two-fold pinch points, one coming from the rank-1 field (spin ice) and another from the rank-2 field (the 𝑬𝖳𝟤+𝖤{\bf\it E}^{\mathsf{T_{2}+E}} field), and cannot be taken on their own as an indication of an emergent rank-2 gauge theory. . This analysis therefore highlights the importance of studying the different accessible scattering channels to expose the anisotropic features associated with the realization of an emergent gauge theory, in addition to the development of an accompanying field theory analysis, as elaborated in Sec. III, to unequivocally identify a spin liquid phase and its underlying gauge theory.

As a final remark, we note that by combining the results summarized by the phase diagrams in Figs. 2, 3, and 5, we have established that all CSLs in Table. 1 are continuously connected without having to pass through any conventional long-range ordered phase in the {Jz​z,J±,J±⁣±,Jz±}\{J_{zz},J_{\pm},J_{\pm\pm},J_{z\pm}\} parameter space. For example, from Figs. 3 and 5, we see that the Kramers CSLs 6, 7, 8 and 9, and the non-Kramers CSL 5 connect to each other. In addition, Fig. 2 shows that all the other non-Kramers CSLs connect to the CSL 5. The parameter space of the CSLs is delineated by a “main body” (i.e. the extended volume phase in parameter space that corresponds to the spin ice state) while various surfaces and lines define the other CSLs that extend out of the body.

So far, we have presented an analysis of the gauge theories describing the low-temperature behavior of all possible CSLs realized by the generic anisotropic nearest-neighbor bilinear Hamiltonian on the pyrochlore lattice. Moreover, we have identified the features in reciprocal space correlation functions that can allow to an identification of those CSLs. In the next section, we present a CMC numerical study of the heretofore unexplored new CSLs identified in this work, namely CSL 6 and CSL 9. In doing so, we compare the CMC results on these models with the predictions obtained from their respective gauge theory and the large-𝒩\mathcal{N} approximation.

VII Beyond Large-𝓝\bm{\mathcal{N}}: Thermodynamics and structure factors from classical Monte Carlo

In this section, we present the results from CMC simulations of the two previously unidentified CSL 6 and CSL 9 discussed in Sec. V. Our simulations confirm that these unidentified CSLs do not exhibit magnetic order down to the lowest temperatures. The complete set of all possible CSLs of the most general nearest-neighbor bilinear Hamiltonian is presented in Table 1. With the exception of CSL 1, all of these CSLs correspond to regions in parameter space where two or more symmetry-breaking ordered phases compete. We note, however, that the identification of a model at such boundaries is not a sufficient condition for a CSL to be realized and stable down to the lowest temperatures. Indeed, the models whose ground state manifold is characterized by a minimal 𝖠𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}} and two additional irrep fields present a symmetry-breaking transition at low temperatures [93]. This transition is not predicted by the field theory which does not fully capture the |𝑺|2=1|{\bf\it S}|^{2}=1 constraint of every spin. We discuss these special cases in Sec. VIII below.

In the following, we present the thermodynamics of CSLs 6, 7, and 9 obtained via CMC simulations. The CSL 7 has already been discussed in Ref. [65], but its dual CSL 6, obtained via Eq. (63), has, to the best of our knowledge, not been discussed before. Although the two CSLs have the same effective theory, their structure factors display drastically different patterns. The same applies to CSL 9, which is dual to HAFM via the same equation (63). We show the specific heat and spin structure factor for the three CSLs marked in Fig. 5 by golden crosses, and whose structure factors are displayed in Fig. 6 in the first (uppermost row), second, and fourth rows.

For our simulations, we considered a system defined with an FCC unit cell composed of 4​L34L^{3} spins with L=10L=10 and updated the system via a Gaussian spin-flip update [109], and an over-relaxation update [95, 110], in addition to averaging up to 1010 independent CMC runs. We performed 8×1048\times 10^{4} thermalization sweeps and 2×1052\times 10^{5} measurement sweeps where we measured the energy, specific heat, and spin structure factors of the systems considered.

Figures 7 and 8 show the eigenvalue (bands) of the interaction matrix in momentum space, the specific heat, and the spin structure factors obtained for the parameters marked by the yellow crosses for the CSL 6 and CSL 7 in Fig. 5, respectively. As expected, and in agreement with the field analysis performed above, the band structure of the corresponding interaction matrices for these systems host four low-energy flat bands in their spectra (resulting from the 8 degrees of freedom and 4 constraints given by the Gauss’s laws), see panel Figs. 7(a) and 8(a). The equivalence between the band structure of these two models is a consequence of the duality of the Hamiltonian [Eq. (1)] via Eq. (63). Neither model shows a sign of a thermodynamic phase transition, as indicated by the smooth evolution of the specific heat of both systems, see Fig. 7(b) and Fig. 8(b). The spin structure factors for both systems are shown in Fig. 7(c)-(d) and Fig. 8(c)-(d) for the (h​h​ℓ)(hh\ell) and (h​k​0)(hk0) reciprocal space planes, respectively, showing excellent agreement with the predictions obtained via large-𝒩\mathcal{N} in Fig. 6.

In addition to the multifold pinch point anisotropies, we note that a distinctive feature in the correlation functions of CSL 7 is the observation of pinch lines, which can be observed in Fig. 8(c) along the [111][111] and symmetry-related directions. In a large-𝒩\mathcal{N} theory, these features are produced by a dispersive band which, along the [111][111] direction, becomes degenerate with the low-energy flat bands, see the first dispersive band marked in red in Fig. 7(a) and Fig. 8(a) 1010 10 The reason behind the observation of the pinch-lines in reciprocal space can be tracked to the degeneracy of the low-energy modes in reciprocal space. In the T→0T\to 0 limit, the spin correlation functions obtained via SCGA is mainly determined by the contributions of the eigenmodes with the smallest eigenvalue. All others become negligible in the T→0T\to 0 limit. In reciprocal space, the pinch-lines are observed for 𝒒{\bm{q}}-points where a dispersive eigenmodes become degenerate with the low-energy modes. This leads to an enhanced intensity along these directions and therefore the observation of pinch lines.. Reference [65] noted that for the CSL 7 singular features (i.e. pinch points) in the reciprocal space correlation function are observed along the location of the pinch line in reciprocal space. In particular, four-fold pinch points can be observed at the intersection of multiple pinch lines. Given that the CSL 6 is dual to the CSL 7, pinch lines should naively be observed in the structure factor of CSL 6. Although it is not immediately clear from the structure factors in Fig. 7(c) and (d) where these features appear, we may track the location of the pinch lines by studying the spin structure factor in the vicinity of a four-fold pinch point. Figure 9 illustrates the spin structure factor for the CSL 6 in the (h​k​Δ​ℓ)(hk\Delta\ell) plane for increasing values of Δ​ℓ\Delta\ell obtained via CMC and the large-𝒩\mathcal{N} method where the intersection of the black dashed lines tracks the location of one of the four pinch lines intersecting at the [220][220] point. We note that, in both CMC and large-𝒩\mathcal{N}, as Δ​ℓ\Delta\ell is increased, the four-fold pinch point (in the (h​k​Δ​ℓ)(hk\Delta\ell) plane with Δ​ℓ=0\Delta\ell=0) splits into four two-fold pinch points. The location of the two-fold pinch points with respect to the four-fold pinch point is consistent with a vector 𝒒=[Δ​ℓ,Δ​ℓ,Δ​ℓ]{\bf\it q}=[\Delta\ell,\Delta\ell,\Delta\ell] and symmetry-related directions, corresponding to 𝒒{\bf\it q} vectors where pinch lines are observed.

Lastly, we present in Fig. 10 the CMC results for CSL 9 corresponding to the dual HAFM model, HAFM*, which is CSL 8. This model presents the same functional form of the energy bands as the regular HAFM where the six low-energy bands of the interaction matrix are flat; see Fig. 10(a). Furthermore, and as found for the HAFM [62], the specific heat of this model presents no sign of symmetry-breaking transition down to the lowest temperatures where it plateaus to a value around the theoretical value 3/43/4  [62, 63]. As in the HAFM, the spin structure factor of the HAFM* exhibits two-fold pinch points, as seen in the (h​k​0)(hk0) scattering plane both in CMC, and as predicted by large-𝒩\mathcal{N}. We further note that the structure factor of the HAFM∗ appears as an intensity-inverted version of that of the HAFM. In other words, the regions of high intensity in the spin structure factor of one model correspond to regions of low intensity in the dual model. This inversion is associated with the precise constraint acting in the ground-state manifold. For the HAFM, this constraint translates to a vanishing single-tetrahedron magnetization (which implies vanishing correlations around the Γ\Gamma points). On the other hand, for the HAFM∗, this constraint allows for a ferromagnetic configuration in the ground-state manifold (which results in a finite intensity at the Γ\Gamma points) and forbids the antiferromagnetic configurations with a non-vanishing 𝖳𝟣,+\mathsf{T_{1,+}} components.

VIII The failed CSL candidates

In this section, we briefly discuss the failed CSL candidates that sit on the boundaries between three magnetically ordered phases but yet present a symmetry-breaking transition at low temperatures. So far we have provided a list of the CSLs stable down to the lowest temperatures and therefore lack any type of conventional symmetry-breaking transition. In the large-𝒩\mathcal{N} approximation, a CSL is realized whenever the lowest band (or bands) of the interaction matrix is flat, resulting in an extensive degeneracy in the ground states. The extensive degeneracy associated with low-energy flat bands in the large-𝒩\mathcal{N} approximation, however, does not impede the onset of an order-by-disorder selection of a symmetry-breaking spin configuration. Such entropically driven selection mechanisms are typically described by high-order terms in the free energy which are not captured by the large-𝒩\mathcal{N} approximation [66]. Consequently, the stability of a CSL must be ascertained using CMC.

It turns out that, broadly speaking, these models are located at the three edges of the green pyramid of the 𝖠𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}} phase (all-in-all-out magnetic order) Fig. 2(a) and Fig. 3 for the non-Kramers and Kramers Hamiltonian, respectively. These edges correspond to models in parameter space where three a𝖷a_{\mathsf{X}} are minimal, with the constraint that one of these minimal fields must be the 𝖠𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}} field. As a shorthand notation, we refer to the models defined on these edges by the minimal irreps describing their ground states, namely, 𝖠𝟤⊕𝖳𝟣,𝗉⊕𝖳𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}}\oplus\mathsf{T_{1,p}}\oplus\mathsf{T_{2}} (where the a𝖠𝟤a_{\mathsf{A_{2}}}, a𝖳𝟣,𝗉a_{\mathsf{T_{1,p}}}, and a𝖳𝟤a_{\mathsf{T_{2}}} are minimal ) [93], 𝖠𝟤⊕𝖤⊕𝖳𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}}\oplus\mathsf{E}\oplus\mathsf{T_{2}} (where the a𝖠𝟤a_{\mathsf{A_{2}}}, a𝖳𝖤a_{\mathsf{T_{E}}}, and a𝖳𝟤a_{\mathsf{T_{2}}} are minimal), and 𝖠𝟤⊕𝖤⊕𝖳𝟣,𝗉\mathsf{A_{2}}\oplus\mathsf{E}\oplus\mathsf{T_{1,p}} (where the a𝖠𝟤a_{\mathsf{A_{2}}}, a𝖤a_{\mathsf{E}}, and a𝖳𝟣,𝗉a_{\mathsf{T_{1,p}}} are minimal) for the non-Kramers case. For the Kramers case, we use the same labeling but replace the 𝖳𝟣,𝗉\mathsf{T_{1,p}} field by 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}} field.

An analysis of the large-𝒩\mathcal{N} interaction matrix bands for the non-Kramers Hamiltonian models reveals that the 𝖠𝟤⊕𝖳𝟣,𝗉⊕𝖳𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}}\oplus\mathsf{T_{1,p}}\oplus\mathsf{T_{2}} model possesses four low-energy flat bands in its interaction matrix spectrum, whereas both the 𝖠𝟤⊕𝖤⊕𝖳𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}}\oplus\mathsf{E}\oplus\mathsf{T_{2}} and the 𝖠𝟤⊕𝖤⊕𝖳𝟣,𝗉\mathsf{A_{2}}\oplus\mathsf{E}\oplus\mathsf{T_{1,p}} models yield two low-energy flat bands. On the other hand, for the Kramers models, both the 𝖠𝟤⊕𝖳𝟣,−⊕𝖳𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}}\oplus\mathsf{T_{1,-}}\oplus\mathsf{T_{2}} model and the 𝖠𝟤⊕𝖤⊕𝖳𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}}\oplus\mathsf{E}\oplus\mathsf{T_{2}} yield two low-energy flat bands, while the 𝖠𝟤⊕𝖤⊕𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{A_{2}}\oplus\mathsf{E}\oplus\mathsf{T_{1,-}} has no flat bands in its interaction matrix spectrum. As previously mentioned, all of these models (with the exception of the 𝖠𝟤⊕𝖤⊕𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{A_{2}}\oplus\mathsf{E}\oplus\mathsf{T_{1,-}} Kramers model) would have been predicted to be a CSL according to the large-𝒩\mathcal{N} analysis. However, a detailed analysis of CMC simulation data for these two models reveals that all of them undergo a symmetry-breaking phase transition at low temperatures (not shown in this paper). We leave the study of details of these failed CSL candidates for future work.

IX Roadmap of quantum phase diagram

In the preceding sections, we systematically investigated the CSLs that arise within the phase diagram of the classical pyrochlore spin system with anisotropic bilinear nearest-neighbor interactions. The parameter regimes in which CSLs appear correspond to regions of maximal frustration where competing interactions suppress conventional magnetic ordering by leaving the energy-minimizing spin configurations underconstrained. This frustration is generally expected to persist upon quantization of the model—except, in cases where quantum order-by-disorder intervenes, analogous to the thermal order-by-disorder mechanisms discussed in Sec. VIII. Deep within classically ordered phases, the corresponding quantum models will typically also exhibit symmetry-breaking long-range order, sometimes stabilized by quantum order-by-disorder, closely resembling their classical counterparts. In contrast, parameter regimes associated with CSLs are much more likely, when carried over to the quantum model, to support quantum spin liquids. These considerations suggest that the classical results presented in this work may serve as a heuristic baseline for further exploration of the corresponding quantum pyrochlore spin systems. In the remainder of this section, we briefly review what is currently known about the quantum phase diagram, in particular for spin-1/21/2, and highlight the regions that remain largely unexplored, including the CSLs that we have identified above.

The best known example is quantum spin ice [6], a form of quantum spin liquid arising from quantum dynamics applied to the classical spin ice model (CSL 1). A large variety of analytical and quantum numerical techniques have been employed to study its physics [43, 111, 21, 32, 38, 37, 35, 36, 40, 42, 88, 112, 51, 52]. Another case with a long history of intensive study is the Heisenberg antiferromagnetic model (CSL 8) [113, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119, 120].

Departing from the above two prototypical classical spin liquids and their quantum counterparts, recent efforts have been made to understand other parts of the phase diagram with high interaction frustration. One of them was targeted at the neighborhood of CSL 4 identified in Ref. [66]. A very recent work [121] explored a one-parameter trajectory in the non-Kramers phase diagram, namely

Jz​z=cos⁡θJ±=−12​sin⁡θJ±⁣±=0Jz±=0\begin{split}J_{zz}&=\cos\theta\\ J_{\pm}&=-\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta\\ J_{\pm\pm}&=0\\ J_{z\pm}&=0\end{split} (68)

which realizes the CSL 1, 2, and 3 for θ∈[−0.1​π,0.25​π]\theta\in[-0.1\pi,0.25\pi], θ∈[0.25​π,0.602​π]\theta\in[0.25\pi,0.602\pi], and θ=0.25​π\theta=0.25\pi, respectively. Furthermore, in the Kramers phase diagram, Ref. [122] studied the Heisenberg plus Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya Hamiltonian with the parametrization

Jz​z=13​(−cos⁡θ−4​sin⁡θ)J±=16​(cos⁡θ−2​sin⁡θ)J±⁣±=13​(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)Jz±=13​2​(2​cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ)\begin{split}J_{zz}&=\frac{1}{3}\left(-\cos\theta-4\sin\theta\right)\\ J_{\pm}&=\frac{1}{6}\left(\cos\theta-2\sin\theta\right)\\ J_{\pm\pm}&=\frac{1}{3}\left(\cos\theta+\sin\theta\right)\\ J_{z\pm}&=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\left(2\cos\theta-\sin\theta\right)\end{split} (69)

which, in the classical model, realizes the CSL 4 and CSL 8 for θ=π+arctan⁡(2)\theta=\pi+\arctan(2) and θ=0\theta=0, respectively. We note in passing that for tan⁡θ=2\tan\theta=2, the parametrization in Eq. (69) yields Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0, which is enforced for the non-Kramers system. More recently, a quantum phase diagram for a 2D region of the Kramers Hamiltonian with Jz±<0J_{z\pm}<0 in the vicinity of CSL 7 was reported in Ref. [123]. Since the phase diagram in that work was parameterized in terms of J1,J2,J3,J4J_{1},J_{2},J_{3},J_{4} (see Appendix B, Eqs. (139)-(142), for the relation between different notation conventions of the exchange parameters), the full range of parameters explored in Ref. [123] cannot be entirely displayed in the phase diagram of Fig. 11(d) (where Jz±J_{z\pm} was fixed to Jz±=−0.1J_{z\pm}=-0.1; see caption of that figure) as the interaction parameter Jz±J_{z\pm} varies as a function of the couplings J1,J2,J3,J4J_{1},J_{2},J_{3},J_{4}. These recent works on QSLs are summarized in Table 4, and their location in the phase classical diagrams indicated in Fig. 11.

To summarize, using a variety of numerical schemes, a number of studies have found evidence for the existence of quantum spin liquid phases that surround locations or regions where the classical spin liquids discussed earlier in this paper are realized. Apart from the extensively studied quantum variants of classical models located near CSL 1 (classical spin ice) and CSL 8 (Heisenberg antiferromagnetic model), very recent results are providing some insight on the possibility of quantum spin liquids in the vicinity of CSL 4 [66] and CSL 7 [123]. By the duality of the Kramers and non-Kramers Hamiltonian in Eq. (63) and Eq. (52), respectively, CSLs 4, 7 and 8 listed in Table  4 are dual to CSLs 5, 6, and 9, respectively. We thus expect the thermodynamic properties and the low-energy effective theories of these last three CSLs to be identical to those of CSLs 4, 7 and 8, respectively. From this brief survey, we note, however, that various regions in parameter space where a CSL is realized have not been systematically studied in the corresponding quantum model. Studying these unexplored regions yields the potential of realizing novel quantum spin liquid as well as non-conventional magnetic orders which are not observed in the classical model [123].

Underexplored quantum region 1: The extent and precise nature of the disordered state observed in the quantum S=1/2S=1/2 model for the {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters corresponding to the CSL 2 [see phase diagram Fig. 2(a)] and its immediate vicinity in the non-Kramers phase diagram has not been fully elucidated. Reference [66] found no conventional magnetic order in the vicinity of the CSL 2 and in the proximity of CSL 3 1111 11 Ref. [66], using energy scale set by Jz​z=3J_{zz}=3, identified a region of no conventional magnetic order for which J±⁣±/Jz​z∈[−0.5,0.0]J_{\pm\pm}/J_{zz}\in[-0.5,0.0] in the vicinity of the line of {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters defining CSL 2, which would also encompass the region J±⁣±/Jz​z∈[0.0,0.5]J_{\pm\pm}/J_{zz}\in[0.0,0.5] by invoking the duality (52). for a finite range of the J±J_{\pm} and J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} parameters. In addition, Ref. [121] reported an absence of magnetic order for the {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters defining CSL 2 [i.e., where J±⁣±=0J_{\pm\pm}=0 and all Jz​zJ_{zz} and J±J_{\pm} values on the classical phase boundary, i.e. red plane in Fig. 11(b)]. Putting the results of Ref. [66] and Ref. [121] together, it is not clear whether the finite range of J±⁣±≠0J_{\pm\pm}\neq 0 for which no order is seen in Ref. [66] (for fixed Jz​zJ_{zz}) extends over the complete classical phase boundary of CSL 2 (of varying Jz​zJ_{zz}, see phase diagram Fig. 2(a)) or whether a quantum spin liquid state with |J±⁣±|≠0|J_{\pm\pm}|\neq 0 is realized only in the vicinity of the {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters of CSL 3. While it seems plausible that the region near CSL 2, but within the CSL 1 (classical spin ice) is a π\pi-flux quantum spin ice [121, 124, 125], the nature of the QSL, or QSLs, in the vicinity of the surface defined by CSL 2 in the phase diagram of Fig. 2(a) is rather unknown at the present time.

Underexplored quantum region 2: Another region of interest in the {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameter space that has not yet been systematically explored in the quantum model is the one connecting CSL 8 and CSL 6 and, by the Jz±→−Jz±J_{z\pm}\rightarrow-J_{z\pm} duality, CSL 9 and CSL 7, respectively [see Fig. 11(c) and (d)]. In other words, the question here is what might the quantum analogue of the classical phase diagram shown in Fig. 5 be. As stated above, CSL 6 and CSL 9 have, to the best of our knowledge, not been studied before and prior to the present work (see Table 1). We first note that a QSL “similar” to CSL 7 was found in the pseudofermion functional renormalization-group (PFFRG) calculations of Ref. [123]. In that work, the anisotropic features observed in the correlation functions of the identified QSL, i.e. pinch-lines as well as twofold and fourfold pinch points, were found to resemble those realized for CSL 7. The observation and resemblance of these features suggest that this QSL is a pinch-line rank-2 quantum spin liquid, i.e. the quantum analogue of the classical pinch-line spin liquid [65]. As discussed in Ref. [123], the pinch lines, twofold and fourfold pinch point features observed in the correlation functions of the quantum model descend from those observed in the classical model, which we discussed in Sec. VI, as shown in the second and fourth row of Fig 6, and in Sec. VII, Fig. 9. On the other hand, Refs. [116, 122] showed, again using PFFRG, that the structure factors of the QSL observed for the {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters corresponding to the CSL 8 (the Heisenberg antiferromagnet) exhibit only twofold pinch points, indicating that the underlying theory for this QSL is described by a rank-1 field – as naively expected [36].

Referring to the classical phase diagram illustrated in Fig. 11(c) and (d), the two QSLs discussed above, that is the quantum pinch-line spin liquid and the quantum Heisenberg antiferromagnet spin liquid, as well as their respective dual partners, may be continuously connected in parameter space by following the path indicated by the black line connecting CSLs 6 and 8 (for Jz±>0J_{z\pm}>0) or CSLs 7 and 9 (for Jz±<0J_{z\pm}<0). These two paths can also be viewed as those indicated in Fig. 5, but without crossing the CSL 5.

To summarize, it would appear worthwhile to study the low-temperature properties of these four presumed QSLs that emerge from CSL 6 (and its dual, CSL 7) and CSL 8 (and its dual, CSL 9) for example, using pseudo Marojana fermion RG [126]. Such an approach would allow to explore the T>0T>0 properties of these models In particular, a detailed exploration of the anisotropic reciprocal space structures of their spin-spin correlations to provide valuable insights into their effective low-energy quantum gauge theory, and how the latter relates or not at T>0T>0 with the classical gauge theories described in the present work.

X Proximity to a classical spin liquid and materials outlook

In this section, we first discuss how the CSLs occupying a zero-measure region of the parameter space at zero temperature control a finite parameter volume at finite temperature, making them relevant to actual materials.

In the previous sections, we identified all CSLs of the most general bilinear nearest-neighbor spin Hamiltonian on the pyrochlore lattice that remain stable down to T=0T=0. As illustrated in Table 1, apart from CSL 1 (classical spin ice) all other T=0T=0 CSLs are restricted to a fined-tuned sub-dimensional manifold of the full four-dimensional {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameter space. However, previous works [57, 64] have shown that systems with couplings {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} close to those of a particular CSL often exhibit signatures above their transition temperature to long-range order – most notably finite-temperature spin structure factors – that resemble those of the nearby CSL. Having noted above that several CSLs can “collide” or “intersect” in the {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameter space (see Fig. 5), and building on the observations of Refs. [57, 64], we illustrate in subsection X.1 below how proximity to two “nearby” CSLs influences the physics of a system in its cooperative paramagnetic regime above the critical temperature where it develops long-range order. In the following subsection X.2, we provide a survey of some rare-earth pyrochlore materials that either naturally reside in the proximity of a CSL, or may be experimentally tuned to lie close to one thanks to departure from perfect stoichiometry.

X.1 An example: all-in–all-out long-range order with adjacent CSL 8 and nearby CSL 6

To illustrate the effects of the proximity of two CSLs on the development of a long-range-ordered phase upon cooling from the paramagnetic phase, we consider, as an example, the phase diagram shown in Fig. 5. We introduce the parametrization (Jz​z,Jz±)=(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)(J_{zz},J_{z\pm})=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta) with θ\theta varying in the vicinity of the value where the CSL 8 is stabilized, i.e. θCSL​ 8≃2.19\theta_{\mathrm{CSL\ 8}}\simeq 2.19, while the remaining J±J_{\pm} and J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} interaction parameters are given by Eq. (54). Figure 12 illustrates the temperature evolution of the thermally averaged 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} order parameter, ⟨|m𝖠2|⟩\langle|m_{\mathsf{A}_{2}}|\rangle, and specific heat, CC, obtained via CMC in panels (a) and (b), respectively. In this figure, the dashed white line serves as a guide to the eye to mark the CSL 6–CSL 8 crossover, obtained by tracking the inflection point of ⟨m𝖠𝟤2⟩\langle m_{\mathsf{A_{2}}}^{2}\rangle evolution 1212 12 One could also identify an additional crossover line between the CLS 8 and the paramagnetic phase obtained via mean-field theory [127] given as the maxm,𝐪​[εm​(𝐪)]/3\rm{max}_{m,\bm{q}}[\varepsilon_{m}(\bm{q})]/3, where εm​(𝒒)\varepsilon_{m}(\bm{q}) are the eigenvalues of the interaction matrix 𝑱μ​να,γ​(𝒒)\bm{J}_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha,\gamma}(\bm{q}). However, this crossover is predominantly above the highest temperature considered in Fig. 12 and is therefore omitted. On the other hand, the solid white line labels the symmetry-breaking transition between the CSL 8 and the 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} long-range ordered phase. For more details on the definitions of these lines, we refer the reader to Appendix E. As shown in panels (a) and (b) of Fig. 12, as θ\theta exceeds θCSL​ 8\theta_{\mathrm{CSL\ 8}}, the system enters the 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} phase, characterized by a non-zero 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} order parameter below a critical temperature Tc​(θ)T_{c}(\theta) where the specific heat displays a sharp peak [indicated by the color bar of Fig. 12(b)].

The effect of tuning the parameter θ\theta on the low-temperature physics of the system can be further exposed by studying the evolution of the spin structure factor, 𝒮⁡(𝒒){\mathcal{S}}({\bf\it q}), as a function of this parameter. Figure 13 illustrates this structure factor for six sets of {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters at temperatures and angles corresponding to those labeled by golden crosses in Fig. 12. In this figure, each row corresponds to a set of correlation functions sampled via CMC in the (h​k​0)(hk0) plane at an angle θ\theta and temperature TT corresponding to the gold crosses in Fig. 12. For panels (a-f) the system is at a finite temperature within CSL 6, where twofold and fourfold pinch point features in 𝒮⁡(𝒒){\mathcal{S}}({\bf\it q}) are observed, as indicated by the white arrows in panels (a) and (b) of Fig. 13, respectively. The presence of fourfold pinch points is a consequence of the effective low-temperature U(1) rank-2 theory describing the spin liquid phase. We note that, as θ\theta increases and the {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters approach those defining CSL 8, the energy cost associated with the 𝖠𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}} field decreases, leading to a (temperature-driven) proliferation of the (progressively decreasing energy) gauge charges associated with this field and, consequently, the broadening of the fourfold pinch points, see Fig. 13(b), (d), and (f). When the system enters the CSL 8 phase, the m𝖠𝟤m_{\mathsf{A_{2}}} field becomes part of the ground-state manifold. In the CSL 8, only twofold pinch points remain, and the effective low-temperature theory is now described by three copies of a rank-1 field, where each field fulfills a U(1) Gauss’ law, see Fig. 13(g-h)

For the two parameter sets which eventually result in long-range all-in/all-out (𝖠𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}}) order, broad pinch point features at temperatures above the critical transition are observed in 𝒮⁡(𝒒){\mathcal{S}}({\bf\it q}), see Fig. 13(i-l). The broad pinch points are associated with the closest CSL, i.e. CSL 8, where the broadness of these reflect a thermal population of the gauge charges associated to the CSL. Indeed, the spin structure factors obtained above the 𝖠𝟤\mathsf{A_{2}} ordered phase do not show the modulation around the ⟨220⟩\langle 220\rangle points associated with the fourfold pinch point observed in the CSL 6 phase, compare Fig. 13(j) and (l) with Fig. 13(b), (d), and (f). As the system approaches the critical temperature Tc​(θ)T_{c}(\theta) from the paramagnetic phase, the pinch point features become sharper (signaling the progressive depopulation of the gauge charges associated with the CSL 8), however, the overall intensity of the correlation function starts to cluster around the points in reciprocal space where sharp magnetic Bragg peaks associated with the 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} order (i.e. the ⟨200⟩\langle 200\rangle and ⟨220⟩\langle 220\rangle points) start to progressively develop, see Fig. 13(j) and (l). We note that the correlation functions shown in Fig. 13(i-l) do not possess features that can be associated with the fourfold pinch points or pinch lines, implying that the physics in the cooperative paramagnetic regime are mainly determined by the closest CSL, which in this case is CSL 8, and not CSL 6. The evolution of the anisotropic features observed in 𝒮⁡(𝒒){\mathcal{S}}({\bf\it q}) as a function of TT and θ\theta therefore indicates that a spin liquid regime prevails above the transition temperature in ordered phases, placing the emergent gauge field description and its associated gauge charges as a natural framework to describe phenomena observed in these temperature regimes.

Although we have considered in Fig. 12 and 13 a specific parametrization of the {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} couplings to illustrate the manifestation of anisotropic features associated to a CSL at a temperature above an ordered phase, similar results generally apply to other CSLs. This suggests that, even though the CSLs we identified are constrained to low-dimensional manifolds in the four-dimensional {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameter space, any model that falls in the vicinity of a CSL will display features associated with the competition characteristic of the proximate CSL at intermediate and high temperatures. As such, our study is not merely on fine-tuned parameters at the zero-temperature phase boundary — it is also relevant to the physics in a finite volume of parameter space near the phase boundary at finite temperature which is strongly influenced by the nearby zero-temperature CSLs.

X.2 Rare-earth pyrochlore materials in close proximity to a CSL

We now ask whether there exist materials with magnetic rare-earth ions on the pyrochlore lattice that lie close to one of the CSLs identified in Sections IV and V. As illustrated in Subsection X.1, a material described by Eq. (1) may, even without being precisely tuned to one of these CSLs, exhibit spin correlations over a finite temperature window that are inherited from that nearby CSL. In this sense, although such a material may ultimately avoid the CSL and instead develop long-range order at low temperatures, an understanding of the emergent gauge fields of the neighboring CSL, particularly their associated temperature-dependent structure factor, remains essential for rationalizing the material’s properties in the collective paramagnetic regime above the ordering temperature. On the other hand, a material whose exchange couplings {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} place it close to a CSL, yet fails to develop long-range order down to the lowest temperatures while exhibiting a structure factor that deviates significantly from the predictions of the corresponding gauge theory, would point to the presence of additional physics. Such effects could arise, for example, from extra interactions (e.g., beyond nearest-neighbor) or from quantum corrections to the classical gauge theory [66]. Observations of this kind would therefore motivate extensions of the theoretical framework developed above. With this perspective in mind, we now turn to a discussion of several insulating rare-earth pyrochlore materials that appear to lie in close proximity to some of the CSLs considered above.

X.2.1 Tb2Ti2O7

Along with the Ho2Ti2O7 and Dy2Ti2O7 spin ice materials [18, 25, 19, 22], Tb2Ti2O7 was one of the first magnetic rare-earth pyrochlore oxide materials found to not develop long-range order down to at least T∼50T\sim 50 mK [128, 16]. Later, in an important work, Taniguchi et al. [129] discovered an extreme sensitivity of the thermodynamic behavior of Tb2+xTi2-xO7+y to its precise stoichiometry. Specifically, it was found that a very slight variation of xx around the stoichiometric value x=0x=0 tunes the system from a spin-liquid state for x≲xcx\lesssim x_{c} to a partially magnetically ordered state for x≳xcx\gtrsim x_{c}, with xc∼−0.005x_{c}\sim-0.005. For x=0.005x=0.005, heat capacity measurements reveal a sharp peak at Tc≈0.5T_{c}\approx 0.5\,K, indicating a phase transition into a state with a small antiferromagnetic ordered moment. Such extreme sensitivity to sample composition suggests that a hidden predominant order, possibly accompanied by a weak antiferromagnetic moment, is realized for x=0.005>xcx=0.005>x_{c} [129]. Subsequent work by the same group [107] suggested that Tb2+xTi2-xO7+y lies near a quadrupolar phase (the proposed hidden order in Ref. [129]) and a QSL, possibly a quantum spin ice phase, with small stoichiometric variations driving the transition between them.

Within the nearest-neighbor model of Eq. (1), with Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0), non-Kramers ions on the pyrochlore lattice admit three quadrupolar long-range ordered phases [35] that correspond to the phases labeled 𝖳𝟣,𝗉\sf T_{1,p}, 𝖳𝟤\sf T_{2} and 𝖤\sf E in the phase diagram of Fig. 11(a). Therein, two triple points are realized; one where 𝖳𝟣,𝗉\sf T_{1,p}, 𝖤\sf E and the spin ice (CSL 1) meet, corresponding to CSL 4, and one where 𝖳𝟤\sf T_{2}, 𝖤\sf E and CSL 1 meet, corresponding to CSL 5. Of note, for the quantum S=1/2S=1/2 version of the model, recent numerical work using PFFRG found an absence of conventional magnetic order at T=0T=0 in an extended {J±/Jz​z,J±⁣±/Jz​z<0}\{J_{\pm}/J_{zz},J_{\pm\pm}/J_{zz}<0\} region that roughly tracks the 𝖳𝟣,𝗉−𝖤\sf T_{1,p}-\sf E boundary and includes the triple point where CSL 4 occurs. By the duality Eq. (52), this corridor without magnetic order would be replicated for J±⁣±/Jz​z>0J_{\pm\pm}/J_{zz}>0 at the 𝖳𝟤−𝖤\sf T_{2}-\sf E phase boundary, including CSL 5, where Tb2+xTi2-xO7+y has been proposed to reside for x≲xcx\lesssim x_{c} [107]. On the other hand, a more recent inelastic neutron scattering work argues, on the basis of an analysis that ignores the quadrupolar interactions between the Tb3+ ions but incorporates the effects of the low-lying crystal field of Tb3+ (at an energy E∼1.5E\sim 1.5 meV [33, 130]), that Tb2Ti2O7 is located at the boundary between several magnetic phases, such as a splayed ferromagnet and antiferromagnetic ones [83]. These magnetic (i.e. conventional dipolar-ordered) phases are not realized for the non-Kramers version of Eq. (1) with Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0. They would, however, somewhat correspond to the phases found for Kramers ions in Fig. 3 for J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} negative (splayed ferromagnet) and positive (antiferromagnet) – such behavior arising due to the incorporation of the excited crystal field states [130] in the model considered in Ref. [83].

While stoichiometric Tb2Ti2O7 may be close to a CSL, it is the small change in stoichiometry in Tb2+xTi2-xO7+y that has allowed this proximity to be exposed by driving a transition from a long-range ordered state to a spin liquid [129]. How the change of stoichiometry causes the ground state transition from a spin liquid to an ordered phase in Tb2+xTi2-xO7+y as xx increases is not understood, but there are likely multiple microscopic mechanisms operating concurrently.

One possible contributing factor is an effective negative chemical pressure, as suggested by the observation [129] that the cubic unit-cell size aa increases as xx increases from x=−0.015x=-0.015 to x=0.01x=0.01. In contrast, the stoichiometric sister compounds Tb2Sn2O7 [131, 132] and Tb2Ge2O7 [133, 134], which respectively have a larger and smaller aa value than Tb2Ti2O7, order both into a Γ9\Gamma_{9} splayed ferromagnetic (SFM) phase 1313 13 Note that a non-Kramers ion system strictly described by Hamiltonian (1) with Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 cannot support such a SFM phase. This follows because the 𝖳𝟣,𝗉\mathsf{T_{1,p}} and 𝖳𝟣,𝗂\mathsf{T_{1,i}} irreps do not mix, corresponding to quadrupolar and magnetic (dipolar) order parameters, respectively. Consideration of the excited crystal electric field levels is therefore necessary to generate the effective couplings required to stabilize such a phase [33, 135, 132, 83].. Moreover, and in paradoxical contrast to the xx-dependence of aa in Tb2+xTi2-xO7+y [129] with ∂a/∂x<0\partial a/\partial x<0, earlier neutron diffraction measurements had found that applying high (positive) pressure (P≳1P\gtrsim 1 GPa, which decreases aa) using sapphire anvil cells induces long-range antiferromagnetic order [136, 137]. How a hypothetically ideal (positive or negative) uniform hydrostatic pressure [137] may change the ground state of Tb2Ti2O7 currently lacks a microscopic explanation. Other mechanisms that are presumably operating in the ground state transition of Tb2+xTi2-xO7+y [129, 107] include: (1) a modification of the Tb3+−-Tb3+ interactions (both their average and their random distribution); (2) the lowering of the local point-group symmetry away from D3​dD_{3d} allowing for additional {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} couplings in Eq. (1); and, perhaps most importantly, (3) the degeneracy-lifting of the ground doublet of non-Kramers Tb3+, an effect minimally described by adding an effective (random, site-dependent) transverse field in Eq. (1) [138, 45]. Which of these effects is predominantly responsible for the ground state change in Tb2+xTi2-xO7+y is an open and interesting question.

Evidence has thus progressively accumulated over the past three decades that Tb2Ti2O7 resides near a CSL, possibly CSL 5 [107], which may be promoted to a quantum spin liquid by quantum fluctuations [66], with sample stoichiometry potentially driving a ground-state transition between a quadrupolar phase and the CSL. While appealing, this interpretation faces several challenges. First, the lowest excited crystal-field doublet of Tb3+ in Tb2Ti2O7 lies only about 1.5 meV above the ground state. This relatively small energy separation renders a description of the material in terms of an effective spin-1/2 model—such as Eq. (1), augmented by long-range magnetic dipole–dipole interactions and obtained by projecting all multipolar Tb–Tb interactions onto the ground doublet while neglecting virtual crystal-field fluctuations (VCFF) [33, 130, 86, 16, 83]—potentially questionable. Second, neutron scattering experiments on various Tb2Ti2O7 samples at temperatures below ∼100\sim 100 mK reveal intense scattering at wave vector 𝒒=(12,12,12){\bm{q}}=\left(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\right) [139, 140]. Such sharp features are not accounted for by the correlations predicted for CSL 5 (see Appendix  G). Accounting for the 𝒒=(12,12,12){\bm{q}}=\left(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\right) correlations has proven challenging, requiring unrealistic very long-range interactions between the SzS^{z} components of the pseudospin-1/2 [140]. However, and interestingly, Ref. [141] has argued that the three-spin interaction generated by VCFF [16] and ignored in Eq. (1) (with Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0) could provide an explanation for those correlations.

After three decades [128] of investigation, it is now abundantly clear that Tb2Ti2O7, along with its finely tuned off-stoichiometric variant Tb2+xTi2-xO7+y, is a highly intriguing compound that harbors strongly competing magnetic and quadrupolar phases and, quite possibly, a quantum-disordered phase—either an intrinsic CSL, such as CSL 5, or one arising from a disorder-induced splitting of the ground-state doublet. With an understanding of the gauge theory describing CSL 5, a strong candidate for an intrinsic CSL realizable in Tb2+xTi2-xO7+y, we now have a valuable conceptual framework to guide the interpretation of future experimental studies and also build upon. In particular, determining to what extent the QSL observed in this compound relates or not to, CSL 5 will help pave the way toward a definitive understanding of this long-standing perplexing material.

X.2.2 Yb2Ti2O7

Heat-capacity measurements on Yb2Ti2O7, revealing a broad anomaly near T∼2T\sim 2 K followed by a sharp peak at Tc∼214T_{c}\sim 214 mK signaling a phase transition, possibly to long-range magnetic order, were first reported nearly sixty years ago by Blöte et al. [142]. The first indication that the low-temperature state of Yb2Ti2O7 may be unconventional was provided by Hodges et al. [143], who confirmed the heat-capacity anomaly, but found no evidence for long-range order from neutron diffraction and muon spin relaxation measurements. This work helped catalyze extensive experimental and theoretical investigations of this compound, along with its sister materials Yb2X2X_{2}O7 (X=Sn,Ge,PtX=\mathrm{Sn},\mathrm{Ge},\mathrm{Pt}), spanning the past twenty-five years (see Refs. [15, 16] for reviews). To this day, the central question regarding Yb2Ti2O7 remains the one posed in Ref. [143]: what is the nature of the state below T∼0.2T\sim 0.2 K?

With Yb3+ being a Kramers ion with a large energy separation of ∼77\sim 77 meV (∼900\sim 900 K) to its lowest excited crystal field level [144] and with its small magnetic moment of ∼2\sim 2 μB\mu_{\textrm{B}}, and thus negligible magnetic dipole–dipole interactions, Yb2Ti2O7 is expected to be well described by Eq. (1). Indeed, a significant effort has been devoted for the past fifteen years to precisely determine the set of {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters for this compound [55, 56, 145, 146, 79]. The most prevalent approach for determining those couplings has been to fit the magnon spectrum obtained from inelastic neutron scattering (INS) measurements on single crystals subject to a large polarizing magnetic field [56, 146, 79]. The currently accepted refined exchange parameters place Yb2Ti2O7 very close to the classical phase boundary between a (splayed) ferromagnetic phase and an antiferromagnetic one — the 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}} and 𝖤{\mathsf{E}} phases, respectively, as illustrated in Fig. 3(b).

Such INS experiments have revealed an intriguing evolution of the magnon excitations as the magnetic field is reduced. Rather than the sharp modes typically expected in a well-ordered magnet, the magnons broaden significantly at lower fields, accompanied by the emergence of relatively flat low-energy bands. This incompletely understood behavior is thought to be linked form of “multiphase competition” [77]—such as the material’s proximity to the 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}} and 𝖤\mathsf{E} phases [79, 145, 147, 148, 146]—the precise mechanism of which is unclear. Moreover, in a manner reminiscent of the situation discussed above for Tb2+xTi2-xO7+y, such proximity to a phase boundary is also believed to underlie the pronounced sensitivity of the heat capacity of Yb2Ti2O7 to its precise stoichiometry, which itself depends sensitively on the details of sample synthesis [15, 149, 150, 151]. However, in contrast to Tb3+, Yb3+ is a Kramers ion and, consequently, local disorder arising from off-stoichiometry does not split the ground-state doublet. That said, such disorder is expected to (1) generate additional {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} couplings through the local lowering of D3​dD_{3d} symmetry and (2) introduce randomness into these {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\}.

As in Tb2Ti2O7, one may also ask about the role of chemical or applied pressure. Beginning with Yb2Sn2O7, which orders into a splayed ferromagnetic state, substitution of Sn by Ti (i.e. Yb2(Ti1-xSnx)2O7) reduces the cubic lattice parameter aa and drives the system into an antiferromagnetic phase over a range of compositions [152]. Upon approaching x∼0x\sim 0, corresponding to Yb2Ti2O7, the material exhibits a splayed ferromagnetic ground state in some samples [152], depending sensitively on synthesis conditions as discussed above. Conversely, starting from Yb2Ti2O7 and substituting Ti by Ge, (i.e. Yb2(Ti1-yGey)2O7) further decreases the lattice parameter as yy increases from 0. This drives the system back into an antiferromagnetic state, even for small yy, that persists up to y=1y=1 [152], as realized in Yb2Ge2O7, which orders in the EE phase below a Néel temperature of 0.57 K [78, 153]. While Yb2Ge2O7 with its smallest aa value orders in the EE phase, neutron diffraction studies on Yb2Ti2O7 under hydrostatic pressure finds that a pressure larger than ∼1\sim 1 kbar causes the systems to order in a splayed ferromagnet (e.g. 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}}) at a critical temperature ∼0.25\sim 0.25K [154]

Thus, similarly to Tb2Ti2O7, the exotic behavior of Yb2Ti2O7 appears strongly related to its proximity to (at least) two competing phases, namely 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}} and 𝖤\mathsf{E}. According to the discussion in Section V, when the 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}} — 𝖤\mathsf{E} boundary collides with the 𝖳𝟤\mathsf{T_{2}} phase it admits a CSL, either CSL 6 or CSL 7 depending on the sign of Jz±J_{z\pm} Assuming that Jz±<0J_{z\pm}<0 for Yb2Ti2O7 [146], the relevant CSL would thus be CSL 7. However, estimates of the {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters for Yb2Ti2O7 [79, 146, 145] all put the material extremely close along the 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}} and 𝖤\mathsf{E} phase boundary, but a fair distance from the location of CSL 7 in the phase diagram [123, 148]. On the other hand, for the quantum S=1/2S=1/2 version of Eq. (1), appropriate to Yb2Ti2O7, both numerical PFFRG [123] and exact diagonalization calculations [148] identify, despite quantitative differences, extended corridors along the 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}}—𝖤\mathsf{E} and 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}}—𝖳𝟤\mathsf{T_{2}} phase boundaries in which conventional long-range magnetic order is absent and finding, instead, an unidentified “non-conventional” emergent quantum phase separating the 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}} splayed ferromagnetic and 𝖤\mathsf{E} antiferromagnetic phases, where Yb2Ti2O7 is believed to reside [77, 148]. Given that the position of Yb2Ti2O7 in the phase diagram appears rather removed from CSL 7, one may ask whether any unconventional quantum state realized at nonzero temperature could nonetheless retain remnants of the SV-R2U1∗ nature of that CSL described (see Sec. V and Table 1) or is a distinct intrinsically quantum phase as recently suggested [148, 123]. In light of the complex behavior exhibited by Yb2Ti2O7 as a function of stoichiometry, whether through slight off-stoichiometry, substitution of Ti by Sn or Ge, or the application of hydrostatic pressure, it is natural to ask whether such perturbations might tune the system closer to this CSL, along with its exotic gauge-theory structure, unconventional low-energy excitations, and rich set of emergent charge-conservation laws. More work, experimental, theoretical and numerical is unquestionably needed to address these interesting and challenging questions.

X.2.3 Er2X2O7 (X=Ti, Ge, Sn, Pt)

Er2X2O7 (X = Ti, Ge, Sn, Pt) is the last family of materials we discuss in this section. These compounds have arguably received less attention than Tb2Ti2O7 and Yb2Ti2O7. In part, this may be because the first systematically studied member of the series, Er2Ti2O7, exhibits a sharp phase transition at TN≈1.2T_{\textrm{N}}\approx 1.2 K [142, 155], with the ordered state correctly identified early on as the antiferromagnetic (𝖤\mathsf{E}) phase [155]. At first glance, this behavior appeared relatively conventional and thus perhaps less likely to warrant extensive further investigation. This perception is, however, misleading. Champion et al. [155] already suggested that Er2Ti2O7, often described as an X​YXY antiferromagnet, similarly to the Yb pyrochlores discussed above [15], could realize the intriguing phenomenon of quantum order by disorder, stabilizing one of the two basis states, ψ2\psi_{2} or ψ3\psi_{3}, of the 𝖤\mathsf{E} irrep (see Fig. 4). Subsequent studies indeed provided compelling evidence that both quantum and thermal order-by-disorder mechanisms cooperate in selecting the ψ2\psi_{2} state in Er2Ti2O7 [156, 157, 95, 158]. 1414 14 It remains unresolved to what extent VCFF effects [33] contribute to the selection of ψ2\psi_{2} in this compound [84, 85, 86].. More recently, Er2Ge2O7 was likewise found to order in the antiferromagnetic 𝖤\mathsf{E} phase [159]. The Néel temperatures of Er2Ti2O7 and Er2Ge2O7, 1.2 K and 1.4 K, respectively, are the highest among the X​YXY pyrochlores [15]. Notably, these two compounds are also unique within X​YXY pyrochlores in that they do not exhibit the broad high-temperature anomaly in the heat capacity at T∈[2,5]T\in[2,5] K, a feature commonly interpreted as evidence of proximity to a competing magnetic phase [15]. This is consistent with the view that they lie deep within the 𝖤\mathsf{E} phase [75].

In contrast to Er2Ti2O7 and Er2Ge2O7, Er2Sn2O7 and Er2Pt2O7 order in the 𝖳𝟤\mathsf{T_{2}} (so-called Palmer-Chalker [97]) phase, with Néel temperatures of 0.11 K [160] and 0.38 K [161], respectively. Both compounds exhibit a broad heat-capacity anomaly in the range T∈[2,5]T\in[2,5] K [15], presumably signaling proximity to either the 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}} or 𝖤\mathsf{E} phase. While it is unambiguous that Er2Sn2O7 orders in the 𝖳𝟤\mathsf{T_{2}} phase [160], a mean-field analysis of neutron diffraction and magnetization data places this compound in a region of exchange-parameter space that straddles the 𝖳𝟤\mathsf{T_{2}}—𝖤\mathsf{E} phase boundary [162]. In that context, one notes that Ref. [163] has proposed that substituting Ti by Sn in the Er2Ti2-xSnxO7 may drive a quantum phase transition separating the 𝖤\mathsf{E} phase found for x≲1.7x\lesssim 1.7 and the 𝖳𝟤\mathsf{T_{2}} in Er2Sn2O7. Interestingly, the aforementioned exact diagonalization [148] and PFFRG [123] calculations had, in addition to a nonconventional quantum phase separating the 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}} and 𝖤\mathsf{E} phases, also found evidence for a range of exchange parameters separating the 𝖳𝟤\mathsf{T_{2}} and 𝖤\mathsf{E} phases where the tendency towards magnetic order may be quite reduced. Moreover, the PFFRG calculations of Ref. [123] found a quantum triple point where the 𝖳𝟤\mathsf{T_{2}}, 𝖤\mathsf{E} and the nonconventional quantum phase meet. One may then ask whether the finite temperature properties and magnon excitations of Er2Sn2O7 and Er2Pt2O77, or Er2Ti2-xSnxO7 as xx is varied, display signatures of this nonconventional quantum phase and perhaps, as for the Yb2Ti2O7 compound, quantum-renormalized relics of the CSL 7 which is located at the classical triple point where 𝖳𝟤\mathsf{T_{2}} (Palmer-Chalker), 𝖤\mathsf{E} and 𝖳𝟣,−\mathsf{T_{1,-}} (splayed ferromagnetic) phases meet, see Fig. 3(b).

The experimental investigation of the above questions are likely to prove challenging and necessitate high-quality single crystals of Er2Sn2O7, possibly studied under high-pressure [154]. However, as such crystals are now available [164], one may perhaps proceed by investigating the magnon excitation spectrum of this material in a magnetic field, similar to the approach taken in Ref. [146] for Yb2Ti2O7.

XI Application to other corner-sharing frustrated-unit lattices

The same construction extends to a broad, well-defined class of corner-sharing frustrated-unit lattices for which the centers of the frustrated units form a bipartite parent lattice and the relevant soft sector occurs at 𝒒=0{\bf\it q}={\bf\it 0}. This class includes the kagomé, checkerboard, and their breathing variants in two dimensions [Fig. 14], as well as the pyrochlore, centered-pyrochlore, and octochlore lattices in three dimensions [Fig. 15]. For a specified Hamiltonian in this class, decomposition of the single-unit Hamiltonian into its complete set of irreps, followed by enumeration of all single-irrep regions, all realizable phase-boundary surfaces, and their lower-dimensional intersections, exhausts the candidate CSL manifolds. The compatibility relations between neighboring units are then used to derive their long-wavelength gauge constraints. The application to the kagomé lattice below demonstrates this procedure explicitly.

We do not claim that this construction exhausts CSLs in Hamiltonians outside this defined class, such as models without the required cluster decomposition, with soft modes away from 𝒒=0{\bf\it q}={\bf\it 0}, or with longer-range or multispin interactions. Such systems require separate extensions of the framework.

Many of these lattices have been studied both theoretically and experimentally. Examples include the kagomé [165, 166, 167, 168, 169, 170], breathing kagomé [171, 172], checkerboard [173, 174, 175], square kagomé [176, 177, 178, 179, 180, 181], breathing pyrochlore [74, 182, 183, 184, 185], octochlore [186], and centered pyrochlore [187] lattices, illustrating the wide range of possible applications of our generalized theoretical framework.

XI.1 General Recipe

Following the approach used above for the pyrochlore lattice, we now recapitulate the general procedure for identifying the set of CSLs stabilized down to zero temperature in a given corner-sharing lattice. This procedure can be divided into five stages, which we describe below.

Stage #​1\#1: Perform an irrep decomposition.
As a starting point, we rewrite the most general bilinear nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian HH in these lattices in the form

H=∑𝗎H𝗎,\displaystyle H=\sum_{\mathsf{u}}H_{\mathsf{u}}, (70)

where H𝗎H_{\mathsf{u}} is the single frustrated-unit Hamiltonian 1515 15 For example, for the kagomé lattice, this would correspond to the Hamiltonian of single triangle, whereas for the octochlore lattice, it would be the Hamiltonian for a single octahedron.. This rewriting can be performed since the lattices considered are corner-sharing with bilinear spin interactions confined to a single frustrated unit 𝗎\mathsf{u}. Using H𝗎H_{\mathsf{u}}, we identify the irreps 𝖷(𝗎)\mathsf{X}^{(\mathsf{u})} and their corresponding energies a𝖷(𝗎)a_{\mathsf{X}}^{(\mathsf{u})} of a single frustrated unit uu, such that the single frustrated-unit Hamiltonian takes the form

H𝗎=∑𝖷a𝖷(𝗎)​|𝒎𝖷(𝗎)|2.\displaystyle H_{\mathsf{u}}=\sum_{\mathsf{X}}a_{\mathsf{X}}^{(\mathsf{u})}|{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{X}}^{(\mathsf{u})}|^{2}. (71)

Here, 𝒎𝖷𝗎{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{X}}^{\mathsf{u}} correspond to the possible conventional magnetic orders observed over the full corner-sharing lattice [57], while the a𝖷(𝗎)a_{\mathsf{X}}^{(\mathsf{u})} are linear functions of the {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters 1616 16 Here, we assume the existence of a diagonal irrep basis yielding this form, which may require an additional diagonalization step, such as that performed in Sec. III.1, to decouple interacting copies of a given irrep.

Stage #​2\#2: Identify sets of interaction parameters.
Using the irrep energies a𝖷(𝗎)a_{\mathsf{X}}^{(\mathsf{u})}, we define the minimal energy of a frustrated-unit ℰ0≡min𝖷​(a𝖷(𝗎))\mathcal{E}_{0}\equiv\mathrm{min}_{\mathsf{X}}(a_{\mathsf{X}}^{(\mathsf{u})}) and identify sets of the {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters where multiple irreps become minimal 1717 17 It is also possible that having a single minimal irrep results in the stabilization of a CSL down to the lowest temperature. For example, this is the case of the CSL 1 in Table 1., i.e. ℰ0=a𝖷1=⋯=a𝖷m\mathcal{E}_{0}=a_{\mathsf{X}_{1}}=\cdots=a_{\mathsf{X}_{m}}. The energy degeneracy between multiple irreps implies the identification of a phase boundary in the T=0T=0 phase diagram between the ordered phases corresponding to the degenerate irreps. As such, the identified points are expected to display a strong competition (i.e., frustration) between the competing magnetic orders.

Stage #​3\#3: Identify the set of parameters with flat bands.
Having identified a set of {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters where multiple irreps achieve minimal a𝖷(𝗎)a_{\mathsf{X}}^{(\mathsf{u})}, we proceed to obtain the band structure in reciprocal space of the full Hamiltonian, i.e.

H=12​∑𝒒∑n=1𝒩×Nμεn​(𝒒)​|𝑺n​(𝒒)|2,\displaystyle H=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\bf\it q}}\sum_{n=1}^{\mathcal{N}\times N_{\mu}}\varepsilon_{n}({\bf\it q})|{\bf\it S}_{n}({\bf\it q})|^{2}, (72)

where 𝒩\mathcal{N} corresponds to the number of spin components, and NμN_{\mu} to the number of sublattices, and 𝑺n​(𝒒){\bf\it S}_{n}({\bf\it q}) is a 𝒩×Nμ\mathcal{N}\times N_{\mu} dimensional eigenvector associated to the band energy εn​(𝒒)\varepsilon_{n}({\bf\it q}). In this stage, we only keep those {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameter sets obtained in Stage #​2\#2 that possess a non-zero number of low-energy flat bands in the spectrum, i.e. εn​(𝒒)=ℰ0\varepsilon_{n}({\bf\it q})=\mathcal{E}_{0}. As previously mentioned, according to an SCGA analysis, all the sets of {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters harboring at least one low-energy flat band could become CSLs.

Stage #​4\#4: Perform a CMC analysis
Next, a CMC analysis of the parameter sets identified in Stage #​3\#3 would allow to verify that no symmetry-breaking transition takes place down to the T→0T\to 0 limit. For this analysis, there are cases where it is crucial to implement some type of cluster-like update, i.e. beyond single spin-flip, to permit a more accurate sampling of the ground-state manifold [66]. It is worth noting that the observation of a symmetry-breaking transition for these parameter sets would imply a thermal order-by-disorder origin as the internal energy associated with the distinct magnetic orders is equivalent 1818 18 This is guaranteed as the irrep energy is equivalent for the competing magnetic orders. and therefore only the entropy term in the free energy function is capable of causing a selection between the competing magnetic orders.

Stage #​5\#5: Derive the long-wavelength theory. After having identified the set of {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} parameters which, according to the CMC study, realize a CSL down to the lowest temperatures, we may next derive the constraints on the ground-state manifold by identifying the set of irreps which become thermally depopulated in the T→0T\to 0 limit. To this end, one would use the irrep modes 𝒎𝖷(u){\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{X}}^{(u)} and construct an expansion as described in Subsection III.2 based on the inter-unit constraints. Interestingly, for any corner-sharing lattices whose interactions can be described by a Hamiltonian on a single frustrated-unit, the constraints on the ground-state manifold will take the form of a generalized Gauss’ law as those presented in Table 1. This is guaranteed for these type of lattices as a band-touching point between the low-energy flat bands and the excited bands takes place at the Γ\Gamma point whenever the number of flat bands is less than the total number of degrees of freedom of the degenerate irreps 1919 19 The only possible alternative is that the number of flat bands is equivalent to the total number of degrees of freedom of the degenerate irreps. In this case, the identified CSL is a “fragile topological” spin liquid [9, 10].. Moreover, one can already identify the type of effective long-wavelength theory describing the low-temperature physics by studying the dispersion away from the band touching point [188].

XI.2 Application to Kagomé Lattice

To demonstrate concretely the implementation of our general framework for identifying CSLs in corner-shared frustrated units, we next present the field-theory derivation for the kagomé lattice. The kagomé unit cell contains three spins, which we take to be those on a triangle defined by the basis vectors

𝒓0\displaystyle{\bf\it r}_{0} =\displaystyle= (0,0),\displaystyle(0,0), (73)
𝒓1\displaystyle{\bf\it r}_{1} =\displaystyle= ad2​(1,0),\displaystyle\frac{a_{d}}{2}(1,0), (74)
𝒓2\displaystyle{\bf\it r}_{2} =\displaystyle= ad4​(1,−3),\displaystyle\frac{a_{d}}{4}\left(1,-\sqrt{3}\right), (75)

where ada_{d} is the distance between the centers of two neighboring triangles. For this lattice, the symmetry group associated to the corner-sharing unit, i.e. a single triangle, is given by the group C3​vC_{3v}. A symmetry analysis of the possible interaction of this lattice identifies the most general bilinear Hamiltonian in the global basis parametrized by the couplings {Jx,Jy,Jz,Dz}\{J_{x},J_{y},J_{z},D_{z}\}, i.e. an XYZ model with an additional DM interaction where the DM vectors are defined along the global zz direction [169], namely

ℋ=∑⟨i​j⟩Jx​Six​Sjx+Jy​Siy​Sjy+Jz​Siz​Sjz+Dz∑⟨i​j⟩(SixSjy−SiySjx).\begin{split}\mathcal{H}=&\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{x}S_{i}^{x}S_{j}^{x}+J_{y}S_{i}^{y}S_{j}^{y}+J_{z}S_{i}^{z}S_{j}^{z}\\ &+D_{z}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}(S_{i}^{x}S_{j}^{y}-S_{i}^{y}S_{j}^{x}).\end{split} (76)

Using the most general nearest-neighbor bilinear Hamiltonian for the kagomé lattice, we give a general overview of how the stages listed in Subsection XI.1 are implemented. In particular, we focus on three CSLs identified in previous works [170, 169], and derive their yet-unidentified effective low-energy theories.

To this end, we follow Stages #​1\#1, #​2\#2, #​3\#3 and #​5\#5, which do not require significant numerical calculations.

Stage #​1\#1: Perform an irrep decomposition
An irreducible representation analysis of this group identifies six distinct irreps [169], namely the {𝖠1,𝖠2​z,𝖠2⟂,𝖤FM,𝖤AFM,𝖤z}\{\mathsf{A}_{1},\mathsf{A}_{2z},\mathsf{A}_{2\perp},\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{FM}},\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{AFM}},\mathsf{E}_{z}\}, leading to the single triangle Hamiltonian of the form

+amix𝒎𝖤FM⋅𝒎𝖤AFM),\displaystyle+a_{\mathrm{mix}}{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{FM}}}\cdot{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{AFM}}}\Big),

This degeneracy if obtained for the set

Jx​y\displaystyle J_{xy} =\displaystyle= −Jz2,\displaystyle-\frac{J_{z}}{2}, (88)
Dz\displaystyle D_{z} =\displaystyle= 3​Jz2.\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{3}J_{z}}{2}. (89)

The third and final triple point is the one for which the 𝖠1\mathsf{A}_{1}, 𝖠2⟂\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}, 𝖤z\mathsf{E}_{z}, and 𝖤AFM\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{AFM}} (the 𝖠1⊕𝖠2⟂⊕𝖤z⊕𝖤AFM\mathsf{A}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}\oplus\mathsf{E}_{z}\oplus\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{AFM}} point) irreps are degenerate, corresponding to the parametrization

Jz\displaystyle J_{z} >\displaystyle> 0,\displaystyle 0, (90)
Jx​y\displaystyle J_{xy} =\displaystyle= Jz,\displaystyle J_{z}, (91)
Dz\displaystyle D_{z} =\displaystyle= 0.\displaystyle 0. (92)

It is worth noting that this last triple point corresponds to the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model. Furthermore, and of particular interest, we note that all of these high-degeneracy points just identified have been studied in previous works [169, 170] where a CSL is stabilized down to the lowest temperature at each one of these points.

Stage #​3\#3: Identify the set of parameters with flat bands
Taking as a starting point the above three triple points identified for the kagomé lattice, one would next study the band structure of the Hamiltonian for these parameters sets. All of the triple points identified have three low-energy flat bands in the matrix spectra and are therefore predicted to realize a CSL according to a SCGA analysis.

Stage #​4:\#4: Perform a CMC analysis
Since the three triple points identified in Stage #\# 2 have already been studied in Refs. [169, 170], which confirmed that these points do realize a CSL phase to the lowest temperatures, we do not carry the CMC analysis and continue with Stage #\# 5 to derive the low-energy theories of these CSLs.

Stage #​5\#5: Derive the long-wavelength theory
As a final stage to exemplify the application of the framework to find all CSLs relevant to the kagomé lattice, we provide the constraints on the ground-state manifold of the CSLs identified in Stage #​3\#3. For this, we consider the CSLs which take place at the 𝖤z⊕𝖤FM⊕𝖤AFM\mathsf{E}_{z}\oplus\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{FM}}\oplus\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{AFM}}, 𝖠1⊕𝖠2⟂⊕𝖤z⊕𝖤FM\mathsf{A}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}\oplus\mathsf{E}_{z}\oplus\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{FM}}, and 𝖠1⊕𝖠2⟂⊕𝖤z⊕𝖤AFM\mathsf{A}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}\oplus\mathsf{E}_{z}\oplus\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{AFM}}, with their corresponding ground-state manifold constraints provided by the coarse-grained theory for the kagomé lattice. The general inter-triangle constraints, equivalent to the inter-tetrahedra constraints in Eq. (26)-(30), yield

m𝖠1=0⟹\displaystyle m_{\mathsf{A}_{1}}=0\implies m𝖠1=ad2(−∂xm𝖤FMy+∂xm𝖤AFMy+∂ym𝖤FMx−∂ym𝖤AFMx)=0\displaystyle m_{\mathsf{A}_{1}}=\frac{a_{d}}{2}\left(-\partial_{x}m_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{FM}}}^{y}+\partial_{x}m_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{AFM}}}^{y}+\partial_{y}m_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{FM}}}^{x}-\partial_{y}m_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{AFM}}}^{x}\right)=0 (93)
m𝖠2⟂=0⟹\displaystyle m_{\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}}=0\implies m𝖠2⟂=ad2∇⋅(𝒎𝖤FM+𝒎𝖤AFM)=0\displaystyle m_{\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}}=\frac{a_{d}}{2}\nabla\cdot\left({{\bf\it m}}_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{FM}}}+{{\bf\it m}}_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{AFM}}}\right)=0 (94)
m𝖠2​z=0⟹\displaystyle m_{\mathsf{A}_{2z}}=0\implies m𝖠2​z=ad2​(∂xm𝖤zx+∂ym𝖤zy)=0\displaystyle m_{\mathsf{A}_{2z}}=\frac{a_{d}}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\partial_{x}m_{\mathsf{E}_{z}}^{x}+\partial_{y}m_{\mathsf{E}_{z}}^{y}\right)=0 (95)
𝒎𝖤FM=0⟹\displaystyle{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{FM}}}=0\implies 𝒎𝖤FM=ad2​(∂xm𝖠2⟂+∂ym𝖠1+∂xm𝖤AFMy+∂ym𝖤AFMx−∂xm𝖠1+∂ym𝖠2⟂+∂xm𝖤AFMx−∂ym𝖤AFMy)=0\displaystyle{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{FM}}}=\frac{a_{d}}{2}\binom{\partial_{x}m_{\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}}+\partial_{y}m_{\mathsf{A}_{1}}+\partial_{x}m_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{AFM}}}^{y}+\partial_{y}m_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{AFM}}}^{x}}{-\partial_{x}m_{\mathsf{A}_{1}}+\partial_{y}m_{\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}}+\partial_{x}m_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{AFM}}}^{x}-\partial_{y}m_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{AFM}}}^{y}}=0 (96)
𝒎𝖤AFM=0⟹\displaystyle{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{AFM}}}=0\implies 𝒎𝖤AFM=ad2​(∂xm𝖠2⟂−∂ym𝖠1+∂xm𝖤FMy+∂ym𝖤FMx∂xm𝖠1+∂ym𝖠2⟂+∂xm𝖤FMx−∂ym𝖤FMy)=0\displaystyle{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{AFM}}}=\frac{a_{d}}{2}\binom{\partial_{x}m_{\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}}-\partial_{y}m_{\mathsf{A}_{1}}+\partial_{x}m_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{FM}}}^{y}+\partial_{y}m_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{FM}}}^{x}}{\partial_{x}m_{\mathsf{A}_{1}}+\partial_{y}m_{\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}}+\partial_{x}m_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{FM}}}^{x}-\partial_{y}m_{\mathsf{E}_{\text{FM}}}^{y}}=0 (97)
𝒎𝖤z=0⟹\displaystyle{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{E}_{z}}=0\implies 𝒎𝖤z=ad2​(∂xm𝖠2​z,∂ym𝖠2​z)=0,\displaystyle{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{E}_{z}}=\frac{a_{d}}{\sqrt{2}}(\partial_{x}m_{\mathsf{A}_{2z}},\partial_{y}m_{\mathsf{A}_{2z}})=0, (98)

where the above constraints are imposed depending on which irreps are not in the ground-state manifold and are therefore expected to be thermally depopulated in the T→0T\to 0 limit. where the electric fields 𝑬(1){\bf\it E}^{(1)} is defined in Eq. (99), and the remaining fields are defined as
