Lastly, for the 𝖠1⊕𝖠2⟂⊕𝖤z⊕𝖤AFM\mathsf{A}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}\oplus\mathsf{E}_{z}\oplus\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{AFM}} point, the ground-state manifold constraints yield

m𝖠2​z=0\displaystyle m_{\mathsf{A}_{2z}}=0 ⟹\displaystyle\implies ∇⋅𝑬(1)=0,\displaystyle{\bf\it\nabla}\cdot{\bf\it E}^{(1)}=0, (109)
𝒎𝖤FM=0\displaystyle{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{FM}}}=0 ⟹\displaystyle\implies {∇⋅𝑬(6)=0∇⋅𝑬(7)=0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}{\bf\it\nabla}\cdot{\bf\it E}^{(6)}=0\\ {\bf\it\nabla}\cdot{\bf\it E}^{(7)}=0,\\ \end{matrix}\right. (110)

where the electric fields 𝑬(6,7){\bf\it E}^{(6,7)} are defined as

𝑬(6)\displaystyle{\bf\it E}^{(6)} =\displaystyle= (m𝖠2⟂+m𝖤AFMym𝖤AFMx+m𝖠1),\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}m_{\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}}+m_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{AFM}}^{y}}\\ m_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{AFM}}^{x}}+m_{\mathsf{A}_{1}}\end{pmatrix}, (111)
𝑬(7)\displaystyle{\bf\it E}^{(7)} =\displaystyle= (−m𝖠1+m𝖤AFMxm𝖠2⟂−m𝖤FMy).\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}-m_{\mathsf{A}_{1}}+m_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{AFM}}^{x}}\\ m_{\mathsf{A}_{2\perp}}-m_{\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{FM}}^{y}}\end{pmatrix}. (112)

We note that the constraints found for all the identified CSLs imply that the ground-state manifolds of these CSLs are all described by three copies of rank-1 U(1) theories – these results being consistent with arguments put forward in Ref. [169]. Having considered the example of the kagomé lattice, we have shown that our framework is readily applicable to other corner-shared frustrated-unit type of lattices whose parent lattice is bipartite (e.g. those illustrated in Figs. 14 and 15), and allowing to identify all CSLs for such models.

XII Discussion and Conclusion

In this work, we have developed a comprehensive framework to identify all CSLs of the nearest-neighbor pyrochlore spin model. Using three independent methods—the coarse-grained field theory, the large-𝒩\mathcal{N} theory, and CMC—we cross-checked all parameter-space manifolds on which ordered phases are degenerate and exhaustively identified the CSL phases.

The resulting nine CSLs in Table 1 therefore exhaust the CSL phases of this Hamiltonian, with no additional CSL remaining elsewhere in its parameter space. This complete map [Figs. 2, 3, and 5] locates each CSL within the surrounding ordered-phase landscape and provides a basis for future theoretical studies and materials searches.

A single microscopic representation also derives the long-wavelength gauge fields and Gauss’s laws of all nine CSLs without separate case-by-case constructions. This identifies two previously unstudied phases, CSLs 6 and 9, and yields new mixed scalar- and vector-charge constraints with associated infinite families of multipole conservation laws. Mapping the full parameter space further reveals the connectivity and evolution of the gauge constraints and the exact dualities between CSLs 6 and 7 and between CSLs 8 and 9 [Eq. (63)], while their microscopic gauge-field embeddings and physical spin correlations distinguish the dual partners. These classification, gauge-theory, and connectivity results were not established previously, and the construction provides a systematic recipe for analogous atlases on the broader lattice class described in Sec. XI.

From the work presented here, we now have in hand a comprehensive overview of all the CSLs on the pyrochlore lattice and how these transform into each other as a consequence of modifying the lowest degenerate irreps by varying the anisotropic bilinear spin-spin couplings. Such insight is crucial for understanding the exotic physics of anisotropic spin models on the pyrochlore lattice, especially for materials that happen to be finding themselves near the phase boundaries of pseudospin long-range order [56, 88, 76, 77, 57, 15]. Furthermore, we have discussed in Sec. IX how the atlas of classical spin liquids in the pyrochlore lattice provides key insights to guide the ultimate construction of a similar atlas for the quantum model, and highlighted various regions of interest for future work. Additionally, we discussed in Sec. X how phenomena typically associated with a CSL phase can be observed at finite temperatures in systems whose interaction parameters {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} lie in proximity of a CSL but ultimately order into a symmetry-broken phase. Our atlas of CSLs on the pyrochlore lattice with nearest-neighbor couplings is a crucial step toward a complete understanding of one of the most representative frustrated magnetic systems.

Lastly, we have illustrated how the same framework used in the identification of the atlas of CSLs on the pyrochlore lattice can be used to identify the CSLs in other corner-sharing lattices with bi-partite parent lattices in two and three dimensions. In particular, we provided a concrete example by applying this framework to the kagomé lattice, and identify the general set of constraints through which the effective low-energy theories for the CSLs in this lattice can be derived.

Appendix B Hamiltonian in the “spin vector basis” and in the global basis

In this appendix, we provide an alternative basis for the general bilinear nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian in the pyrochlore lattice in Eq. (1) [55]. Doing so will further emphasize how the form of the spin Hamiltonian appears significantly different when considering the dual forms discussed above. The Hamiltonian can be parametrized in what we refer to as a “spin vector interaction” basis (SVI) basis with Heisenberg JJ, local Ising JIsingJ_{\rm Ising}, pseudo-dipole JPDJ_{\rm PD}, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) JDMJ_{\rm DM} interactions [84, 55]. In this SVI basis, the Hamiltonian in Eq (1) reads

ℋ\displaystyle\mathcal{H} =\displaystyle= ℋHeis+ℋIsing+ℋPD+ℋDM\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm Heis}+\mathcal{H}_{\rm Ising}+\mathcal{H}_{\rm PD}+\mathcal{H}_{\rm DM} (125)
ℋHeis\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm Heis} =\displaystyle= J​∑⟨i​j⟩𝑺i⋅𝑺j\displaystyle J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}{\bf\it S}_{i}\cdot{\bf\it S}_{j} (126)
ℋz​z\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{zz} =\displaystyle= JIsing​∑⟨i​j⟩(𝑺i⋅𝒛i)​(𝑺j⋅𝒛j)\displaystyle J_{\rm Ising}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\left({\bf\it S}_{i}\cdot{\bf\it z}_{i}\right)\left({\bf\it S}_{j}\cdot{\bf\it z}_{j}\right) (127)
ℋPD\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm PD} =\displaystyle= JPD​∑⟨i​j⟩(𝑺i⋅𝒓i​j)​(𝒓i​j⋅𝑺j)\displaystyle J_{\rm PD}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\left({\bf\it S}_{i}\cdot{\bf\it r}_{ij}\right)\left({\bf\it r}_{ij}\cdot{\bf\it S}_{j}\right) (128)
ℋDM\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm DM} =\displaystyle= JDM​∑⟨i​j⟩𝒅i​j⋅(𝑺i×𝑺j),\displaystyle J_{\rm DM}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}{\bf\it d}_{ij}\cdot({\bf\it S}_{i}\times{\bf\it S}_{j}), (129)

where the spins 𝑺i{\bf\it S}_{i} are here defined in the global Cartesian basis, 𝒛i{\bf\it z}_{i} is the local-zz (cubic [111][111]) direction at the iith lattice site, 𝒓i​j{\bf\it r}_{ij} is the separation vector between lattices sites ii and jj, and 𝒅i​j{\bf\it d}_{ij} labels the direct DM vectors

𝒅03\displaystyle{\bf\it d}_{03} =\displaystyle= (−1,1,0),𝒅02=(1,0,−1),\displaystyle(-1,1,0),\quad{\bf\it d}_{02}=(1,0,-1), (130)
𝒅01\displaystyle{\bf\it d}_{01} =\displaystyle= (0,−1,1),𝒅32=(0,1,1),\displaystyle(0,-1,1),\quad{\bf\it d}_{32}=(0,1,1), (131)
𝒅31\displaystyle{\bf\it d}_{31} =\displaystyle= (−1,0,−1),𝒅21=(1,1,0).\displaystyle(-1,0,-1),\quad{\bf\it d}_{21}=(1,1,0). (132)

as defined in Ref. [122]. The relation between the interaction parameters basis {Jz​z,J±,J±⁣±,Jz±}\{J_{zz},J_{\pm},J_{\pm\pm},J_{z\pm}\} and the above {J,JIsing,JPD,JDM}\{J,J_{\rm Ising},J_{\rm PD},J_{\rm DM}\} basis yields

J\displaystyle J =\displaystyle= 2​(J±+J±⁣±),\displaystyle 2(J_{\pm}+J_{\pm\pm}), (133)
JIsing\displaystyle J_{\rm Ising} =\displaystyle= −10​J±−2​J±⁣±+4​2​Jz±+Jz​z,\displaystyle-10J_{\pm}-2J_{\pm\pm}+4\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm}+J_{zz}, (134)
JPD\displaystyle J_{\rm PD} =\displaystyle= −4​(2​J±+J±⁣±−2​Jz±),\displaystyle-4(2J_{\pm}+J_{\pm\pm}-\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm}), (135)
JDM\displaystyle J_{\rm DM} =\displaystyle= −4​J±+2​Jz±.\displaystyle-4J_{\pm}+\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm}. (136)

Consider now the duality between CSL 8 and CSL 9 that is generated upon the change of sign of Jz±J_{z\pm}. In SVI basis, the former is simply an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model, namely {J,JIsing,JPD,JDM}={32​Jz±,0,0,0}\{J,J_{\rm Ising},J_{\rm PD},J_{\rm DM}\}=\{\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}J_{z\pm},0,0,0\}, while the CSL 9 is a model where all parameters in the SVI basis are non-vanishing, i.e. {J,JIsing,JPD,JDM}={−32​Jz±,8​2​Jz±,8​2​Jz±,2​2​Jz±}\{J,J_{\rm Ising},J_{\rm PD},J_{\rm DM}\}=\{-\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}J_{z\pm},8\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm},8\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm},2\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm}\}. We further note that, in addition to the local basis, i.e. {Jz​z,J±,J±⁣±,Jz±}\{J_{zz},J_{\pm},J_{\pm\pm},J_{z\pm}\}, and the SVI basis, {J,JIsing,JPD,JDM}\{J,J_{\rm Ising},J_{\rm PD},J_{\rm DM}\}, a global parameter basis, namely {J1,J2,J3,J4}\{J_{1},J_{2},J_{3},J_{4}\} is also extensively used in the literature. In the global basis, the spin components are expressed in global Cartesian coordinates, and the spin Hamiltonian takes the form

H𝖾𝗑=∑⟨i​j⟩𝑺i⋅𝒥i​j⋅𝑺j,\displaystyle H_{\sf ex}=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}{\bf\it S}_{i}\cdot\mathcal{J}_{ij}\cdot{\bf\it S}_{j}, (137)

where the exchange matrix 𝒥i​j\mathcal{J}_{ij} couples the spins at the ii and jj sites. For instance, for sublattices 00 and 11, this exchange matrix takes the form

𝒥01=(J2J4J4−J4J1J3−J4J3J1),\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{01}=\begin{pmatrix}J_{2}&J_{4}&J_{4}\\ -J_{4}&J_{1}&J_{3}\\ -J_{4}&J_{3}&J_{1}\end{pmatrix}, (138)

while all other exchange matrices can be obtained by applying the transformation of the single tetrahedron group TdT_{d}. For the explicit form of these exchange matrices we refer the reader to Ref. [57]. The relationship between the local and the global basis is given by the transformation

J1\displaystyle J_{1} =\displaystyle= 13​(−Jz​z+4​J±+2​J±⁣±+2​2​Jz±),\displaystyle\frac{1}{3}\left(-J_{zz}+4J_{\pm}+2J_{\pm\pm}+2\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm}\right), (139)
J2\displaystyle J_{2} =\displaystyle= 13​(Jz​z−4​J±+4​J±⁣±+4​2​Jz±),\displaystyle\frac{1}{3}\left(J_{zz}-4J_{\pm}+4J_{\pm\pm}+4\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm}\right), (140)
J3\displaystyle J_{3} =\displaystyle= 13​(−Jz​z−2​J±−4​J±⁣±+2​2​Jz±),\displaystyle\frac{1}{3}\left(-J_{zz}-2J_{\pm}-4J_{\pm\pm}+2\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm}\right), (141)
J4\displaystyle J_{4} =\displaystyle= 13​(−Jz​z−2​J±+2​J±⁣±−2​Jz±).\displaystyle\frac{1}{3}\left(-J_{zz}-2J_{\pm}+2J_{\pm\pm}-\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm}\right). (142)

In the global basis, the parametrization of the CSL 8 and 9 is given by {J1,J2,J3,J4}={3​Jz±2,3​Jz±2,0,0}\{J_{1},J_{2},J_{3},J_{4}\}=\{\frac{3J_{z\pm}}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{3J_{z\pm}}{\sqrt{2}},0,0\} and {J1,J2,J3,J4}={−Jz±3​2,7​Jz±3​2,4​2​Jz±3,−2​2​Jz±3}\{J_{1},J_{2},J_{3},J_{4}\}=\{-\frac{J_{z\pm}}{3\sqrt{2}},\frac{7J_{z\pm}}{3\sqrt{2}},\frac{4\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm}}{3},-\frac{2\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm}}{3}\}, respectively.

Appendix C Irreducible representations and their exchange coefficients in the global basis

In the main text, we discussed the degeneracy of different magnetic orders using the irrep description with the spin degrees of freedom expressed in the local basis. In this appendix, we provide the irrep modes {𝒎𝖷}\{{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{X}}\} in the global Cartesian basis as well as their exchange coefficients, a𝖷a_{\mathsf{X}}, in the global and in SVI basis above. Table 7 gives the irrep modes in terms of the spin DOFs defined in the global basis while Table 8 gives the exchange coefficients, a𝖷a_{\mathsf{X}}, in terms of the global and SVI basis.

Appendix D Correlation functions

In this appendix, we provide the expressions for the correlation functions presented in the main text. In reciprocal space, and for a generic non-Bravais lattice with a sublattice structure, the general correlation between spins is given by the expression

𝒮μ​να​γ=⟨Sμα​(𝒒)​Sνγ​(−𝒒)⟩,\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{\alpha\gamma}_{\mu\nu}=\langle S_{\mu}^{\alpha}({\bf\it q})S_{\nu}^{\gamma}(-{\bf\it q})\rangle, (143)

where μ,ν\mu,\nu label the sublattices and α,β\alpha,\beta label the spin components. In particular, we compute the additive contribution of the spin-component diagonal elements of the general correlation function

𝒮⁡(𝒒)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}({\bf\it q}) =\displaystyle= ∑α∑μ,ν𝒮μ​να​α\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{\mu,\nu}\mathcal{S}^{\alpha\alpha}_{\mu\nu} (144)
=\displaystyle= ∑α∑μ,ν⟨Sμα​(𝒒)​Sνα​(−𝒒)⟩,\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{\mu,\nu}\langle S_{\mu}^{\alpha}({\bf\it q})S_{\nu}^{\alpha}(-{\bf\it q})\rangle,

which, for short, we refer simply to as the spin structure factor. In addition to the spin structure factor, we have also computed the experimentally measurable unpolarized neutron structure factor, given by the expression

𝒮⟂​(𝒒)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\perp}({\bf\it q}) =\displaystyle= ∑α,β∑μ,ν(δα,β−𝒒^α​𝒒^β)​⟨mμα​(𝒒)​mνβ​(−𝒒)⟩,\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\sum_{\mu,\nu}\left(\delta_{\alpha,\beta}-\hat{{\bf\it q}}^{\alpha}\hat{{\bf\it q}}^{\beta}\right)\langle m_{\mu}^{\alpha}({\bf\it q})m_{\nu}^{\beta}(-{\bf\it q})\rangle, (145)

which measures the correlation between the magnetic moments, 𝒎i​μ{\bf\it m}_{i\mu}, of the systems considered where the sub-index ii labels the primitive FCC vectors 𝑹i{\bf\it R}_{i} and μ\mu denotes the sublattice sites. The relationship between the magnetic moments and the spin degrees of freedom is provided by an anisotropic gg-tensor

mi​μα=∑βgμα​β​Si​μβ,\displaystyle m_{i\mu}^{\alpha}=\sum_{\beta}g_{\mu}^{\alpha\beta}S_{i\mu}^{\beta}, (146)

where gμα​βg_{\mu}^{\alpha\beta} are the components of the gg-tensor associated to the μ\mu-sublattice.

In addition to the unpolarized neutron structure factor, we have also considered the polarized neutron structure factor defined in terms of the incident neutrons’ polarization z^N\hat{z}_{\textrm{N}} [102]. This polarization analysis separates the neutron structure factor in Eq. (145) into two channels, the non-spin-flip (NSF) channel which studies the correlations that are parallel to the incident polarization z^N\hat{z}_{\textrm{N}}

𝒮⟂NSF​(𝒒)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\perp}^{\mathrm{NSF}}({\bf\it q}) =\displaystyle= ∑α,β∑μ,ν(z^Nα​z^Nβ)​⟨mμα​mνβ⟩,\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\sum_{\mu,\nu}\left(\hat{z}_{\textrm{N}}^{\alpha}\hat{z}_{\textrm{N}}^{\beta}\right)\langle m_{\mu}^{\alpha}m_{\nu}^{\beta}\rangle, (147)

and the spin-flip channel which is the complement of the NSF channel, defined as

𝒮⟂SF​(𝒒)=𝒮⟂​(𝒒)−𝒮⟂NSF​(𝒒).\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\perp}^{\mathrm{SF}}({\bf\it q})=\mathcal{S}_{\perp}({\bf\it q})-\mathcal{S}_{\perp}^{\mathrm{NSF}}({\bf\it q}). (148)

We note that the introduction of an anisotropic gg-tensor in Eqs. (145)-(147) effectively “distorts” in momentum (𝒒{{\bf\it q}}) space the correlation functions we have presented [108, 96, 66] which were considered to discernibly expose the underlying gauge theory. For this reason, when reporting in the main text neutron structure factors (e.g. see Fig. 6), we chose an isotropic gg-tensor (i.e. gμα​β=g​δα​βg_{\mu}^{\alpha\beta}=g\delta_{\alpha\beta}). To reiterate, in doing so, we make no assumptions on the nature (Kramers or non-Kramers) of the spin degrees of freedom in order to more clearly expose the underlying gauge theory of the CSLs considered.

Appendix E Determination of the phase transitions and crossovers between distinct CSLs

In Sec. X we illustrate a phase diagram in Fig. 12 (a) and (b) where we identify three distinct phases; two CSL phases and one 𝒒=0{\bf\it q}=0 symmetry-breaking phase. The boundary between the CSL 8 and the symmetry-breaking 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} phase, marked by a white line in Fig. 12 (a) and (b), is identified by tracking the peak of the specific heat

C=⟨ℋ2⟩−⟨ℋ⟩2N​kB​T2,\displaystyle C=\frac{\langle\mathcal{H}^{2}\rangle-\langle\mathcal{H}\rangle^{2}}{Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T^{2}}, (149)

where ⟨⋯⟩\langle\mathcal{\cdots}\rangle signifies a thermodynamic average NN is the number of spins in the system, and kBk_{\mathrm{B}} is the Boltzmann constant which is set to 11. In contrast to the symmetry-breaking transition, the measured specific heat does not show any distinctive feature separating the two CSLs. To estimate the crossover between these two CSLs, we follow a similar approach to the one taken in Ref. [64] where we measure the thermodynamic expectation of the square of the m𝖠2m_{\mathsf{A}_{2}} parameter, namely ⟨m𝖠22⟩\langle m_{\mathsf{A}_{2}}^{2}\rangle, and identity the point of inflection as shown in Fig. 16. We use this quantity to signal the crossover between CSL 8 and CSL 6. The motivation for doing so is that the m𝖠𝟤m_{\mathsf{A_{2}}} field corresponds to the scalar charge excitation associated to the CSL 6, which becomes thermally depopulated as the system crosses over into the CSL 6 regime. We measure the square of the 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} parameter so that we have a measure of how many charges (positive and negative) are still present in the system.

Appendix F Comparison between coarse-grained theory and large-𝒩\mathcal{N} theory

In this section, we provide a comparison between the coarse-grained field theory deducted from the inter-tetrahedra constraint and the large-𝒩\mathcal{N} SCGA results (the latter has been cross-checked with CMC extensively in the main text). We consider a concrete example of the CSL 6. Its low-energy coarse-grained theory identifies the rank-2 field 𝑬𝖲𝖵{\bf\it E}^{\mathsf{SV}}, defined as

𝑬𝖲𝖵=(2​mE13​mT2z−3​mT2y−3​mT2z−mE1+3​mE23​mT2x3​mT2y−3​mT2x−mE1−3​mE2)−3​sin⁡ϕ​(0mT1,−zmT1,−ymT1,−z0mT1,−xmT1,−ymT1,−x0).\begin{split}{\bf\it E}^{\mathsf{SV}}=&\begin{pmatrix}2m_{\text{E}}^{1}&\sqrt{3}m_{T_{2}}^{z}&-\sqrt{3}m_{T_{2}}^{y}\\ -\sqrt{3}m_{T_{2}}^{z}&-m_{\text{E}}^{1}+\sqrt{3}m_{\text{E}}^{2}&\sqrt{3}m_{T_{2}}^{x}\\ \sqrt{3}m_{T_{2}}^{y}&-\sqrt{3}m_{T_{2}}^{x}&-m_{\text{E}}^{1}-\sqrt{3}m_{\text{E}}^{2}\end{pmatrix}\\ &-3\sin\phi\begin{pmatrix}0&m_{T_{1,-}}^{z}&m_{T_{1,-}}^{y}\\ m_{T_{1,-}}^{z}&0&m_{T_{1,-}}^{x}\\ m_{T_{1,-}}^{y}&m_{T_{1,-}}^{x}&0\end{pmatrix}.\end{split} (150)

which fulfills two constraints

m𝖠𝟤=0⟹\displaystyle m_{\mathsf{A_{2}}}=0\implies |ϵi​j​k|​∂iEj​k𝖲𝖵=0,\displaystyle|\epsilon^{ijk}|\partial_{i}E_{jk}^{\mathsf{SV}}=0, (151)
𝒎𝖳𝟣,+=0⟹\displaystyle{\bf\it m}_{\mathsf{T_{1,+}}}=0\implies ∂iEi​j𝖲𝖵=0.\displaystyle\partial_{i}E_{ij}^{\mathsf{SV}}=0. (152)

We can thus write down the low-energy effective Hamiltonian as

ℋCSL6=∫d​v​(|ϵi​j​k|​∂iEj​k𝖲𝖵)2+∂iEi​j𝖲𝖵​∂kEk​j𝖲𝖵\mathcal{H}_{\text{CSL6}}=\int\mathrm{d}v\ (|\epsilon^{ijk}|\partial_{i}E_{jk}^{\mathsf{SV}})^{2}+\partial_{i}E_{ij}^{\mathsf{SV}}\partial_{k}E_{kj}^{\mathsf{SV}} (153)

which, in Fourier space, can be expressed as

ℋCSL6=∫d3​q​EI𝖲𝖵​HI​J​(𝒒)​EJ𝖲𝖵\mathcal{H}_{\text{CSL6}}=\int\mathrm{d}^{3}q\ E_{I}^{\mathsf{SV}}H_{IJ}({\bf\it q})E_{J}^{\mathsf{SV}} (154)

Here, EI𝖲𝖵E_{I}^{\mathsf{SV}} is introduced to organize the degree of freedoms in Ei​j𝖲𝖵E_{ij}^{\mathsf{SV}} in a vector form. HI​J​(𝒒)H_{IJ}({\bf\it q}) is the interaction matrix in the Fourier transformed momentum space. It has four flat bands at the bottom, because there are 8 degrees of freedom in Ei​j𝖲𝖵E_{ij}^{\mathsf{SV}} and 4 scalar constraints. The equal time correlation function ⟨Ei​j𝖲𝖵​(𝒒)​Ek​l𝖲𝖵​(−𝒒)⟩\langle E_{ij}^{\mathsf{SV}}({\bf\it q})E_{kl}^{\mathsf{SV}}(-{\bf\it q})\rangle and ⟨mXα​(𝒒)​mXα​(−𝒒)⟩\langle m_{X}^{\alpha}({\bf\it q})m_{X}^{\alpha}(-{\bf\it q})\rangle can then be extracted from the eigenvectors of the four bottom flat bands.

In parallel, one can compute the same correlation functions from large-𝒩\mathcal{N} which, as shown in Fig. 9, is found to be in good agreement with CMC simulations. In Fig. 17, we illustrate the comparison between the irrep correlation functions ⟨m𝖤1​(𝒒)​m𝖤1​(−𝒒)⟩\langle m_{\mathsf{E}}^{1}({\bf\it q})m_{\mathsf{E}}^{1}(-{\bf\it q})\rangle and ⟨m𝖳2z​(𝒒)​m𝖳2z​(−𝒒)⟩\langle m_{\mathsf{T}_{2}}^{z}({\bf\it q})m_{\mathsf{T}_{2}}^{z}(-{\bf\it q})\rangle obtained via the coarse-grained theory and large-𝒩\mathcal{N} in the T→0T\to 0 limit. We observe an excellent agreement between the two methods. This provides numerical proof of the validity of the coarse-grained theory framework we have developed.

Appendix G Dependence of the neutron structure factors of the CSL 5 as a function of the gg-factor.

In this section, we report the large-𝒩\mathcal{N} calculations of the unpolarized neutron structure factors obtained for the CSL 5 for various choices of the magnetic gg-tensor. CSL 5 is realized in a plane in parameter space {Ju​v}\{J_{uv}\} defined by the constraint Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0. This plane is most naturally realized for the non-Kramers pyrochlores, where the local-zz of the magnetic moments transforms as a dipole, whereas the remaining transverse degree of freedoms transform as quadrupoles. As these degrees of freedom are respectively time odd and time even, they do not couple at the bilinear level, hence requiring Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0. Moreover, in terms of the local gg-tensor, defined as

gLocal=(g⟂000g⟂000gz​z),\displaystyle g_{\rm Local}=\begin{pmatrix}{g}_{\perp}&0&0\\ 0&{g}_{\perp}&0\\ 0&0&{g}_{zz}\end{pmatrix}, (155)

non-Kramers ions would normally be characterized by a vanishing g⟂g_{\perp} reflecting the nature of an isolated non-Kramers crystal field ground doublet. However, it is of interest to explore how virtual crystal-field fluctuations in Tb3+ may engender an effective transverse magnetic response with g⟂≠0g_{\perp}\neq 0 [189], thereby modifying the neutron-scattering form factor that would arise if g⟂g_{\perp} were set to zero. Figure 18 illustrates the dependence of the unpolarized neutron structure factor on g⟂g_{\perp}, computed using the large-𝒩\mathcal{N} method.

For g⟂=0g_{\perp}=0, the neutron scattering structure factor shows the typical pattern of classical Ising spin ice since the transverse spin correlator that would exist at the CSL 5 (DQQ∗ point) [66] is extinguised by g⟂=0g_{\perp}=0. As g⟂g_{\perp} increases, the pattern gets progressively modified (e.g. g⟂=0.5​gz​zg_{\perp}=0.5g_{zz}) exposing additional pinch point features originating from the correlations between the x​yxy spin degrees of freedom (see for example the twofold pinch points in the [h​h​ℓ][hh\ell] plane at [220][220].). These additional features become more prominent as the value of g⟂g_{\perp} is tuned to that of gz​zg_{zz} (e.g. g⟂=gz​zg_{\perp}=g_{zz}), i.e. where the local gg-tensor becomes isotropic. Most importantly, and the main point of performing the calculations reported in this appendix, unlike what has been observed experimentally in Tb2Ti2O7 [139, 140], no evidence of correlations at 𝒒=(12​12​12){\bm{q}}=(\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{2}) are observed in the calculations (Fig. 18).
